arguments.content:
name: tests

on:
  push:
    branches:
    - main
    - 'maint/**'
    tags: [ 'v*' ]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    # Mondays 06:00 UTC -- catches breakage from new upstream releases (numpy, pandas, ...)
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'
  workflow_dispatch: ~

permissions:
   contents: read

concurrency:
   group: tests-${{ github.ref }}
   cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK: 1
  PY_COLORS: "1"
  FORCE_COLOR: 1
  # nox re-uses venvs between sessions when this is set; uv makes venv creation ~10x faster
  NOX_DEFAULT_VENV_BACKEND: uv
  HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE: ci


jobs:

  pre-commit:
    name: pre-commit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: pre-commit/action@v3.0.1
        with:
          extra_args: --all-files --show-diff-on-failure

  test:
    name: py${{ matrix.python-version }} / ${{ matrix.os }}
    needs: pre-commit
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 30
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.9', '3.10', 3.11, "3.12", '3.13-dev']
        os: [
            ubuntu-latest,
            macos-latest,     # arm64 since 2024-04, see #412
            windows-latest
          ]
        include:
          # PyPy only on linux, it's slow enough already
          - python-version: 'pypy3.10'
            os: ubuntu-latest
            experimental: true

          # "oldest supported dependencies" job
          - python-version: 3.10      # FIXME: unquoted -> YAML float 3.1, so this spins up Python 3.1 (!!) instead of extending the 3.10 job
            os: ubuntu-20.04
            deps: minimum

          - python-version: '3.13-dev'
            os: ubuntu-latest
            experimental: true
        exclude:
          - python-version: '3.13-dev'
            os: windows-latest
          # no 3.9 build for macos arm64 in setup-python
          - { python-version: '3.9', os: macos-latest }
          - {python-version: '3.13-dev',os: macos-latest}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # setuptools-scm needs the tags

      - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          allow-prereleases: true
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: |
            pyproject.toml
            requirements/*.txt

      - name: Install
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip wheel
          python -m pip install -e ".[test]"
          python -m pip install nox uv

      - name: Pin minimum versions
        if: matrix.deps == 'minimum'
        run: python -m pip install -r requirements/minimum.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: nox -s tests-${{ matrix.python-version }} -- --cov --cov-report=xml -n auto
        continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}
        env:
          ACME_TEST_NETWORK: off
          ACME_CACHE_DIR: null

      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: ./coverage.xml
          flags: ${{ runner.os }},py${{ matrix.python-version }}
          fail_ci_if_error: ${{ github.event_name != 'pull_request' }}
          verbose: TRUE

      - name: Job summary
        if: always()
        shell: bash
        run: |+
          echo "### ${{ matrix.os }} / Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "* status: **${{ job.status }}**" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "* deps: ${{ matrix.deps || 'latest' }}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"


  docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: "3.12", cache: pip}
    - run: python -m pip install -e ".[docs]"
    - name: Build docs (warnings are errors)
      run: sphinx-build -W --keep-going -b html -d docs/_build/doctrees docs docs/_build/html
    - name: Linkcheck
      if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
      run: sphinx-build -b linkcheck docs docs/_build/linkcheck
      continue-on-error: yes
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: docs-html
        path: docs/_build/html

  build:
    name: Build sdist + wheel
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
         with:
           fetch-depth: 0
       - run: pipx run build
       - run: pipx run twine check --strict dist/*
       - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
         with:
           name: dist
           path: dist/
           if-no-files-found: error



  publish:
    name: Publish to PyPI
    needs: [test, docs, build]
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: { name: pypi, url: https://pypi.org/p/acme-toolkit }
    permissions:
      id-token: write   # trusted publishing -- no API token needed
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - name: Publish
        uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1
        with:
          print-hash: true
          # repository-url: https://test.pypi.org/legacy/
          skip-existing: null

          python -m pip install -e ".[test]"
          python -m pip install nox uv

      - name: Pin minimum versions
        if: matrix.deps == 'minimum'
        run: python -m pip install -r requirements/minimum.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: nox -s tests-${{ matrix.python-version }} -- --cov --cov-report=xml -n auto
        continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}
        env:
          ACME_TEST_NETWORK: off
          ACME_CACHE_DIR: null

      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: ./coverage.xml
          flags: ${{ runner.os }},py${{ matrix.python-version }}
          fail_ci_if_error: ${{ github.event_name != 'pull_request' }}
          verbose: TRUE

      - name: Job summary
        if: always()
        shell: bash
        run: |+
          echo "### ${{ matrix.os }} / Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "* status: **${{ job.status }}**" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "* deps: ${{ matrix.deps || 'latest' }}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"


  docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: "3.12", cache: pip}
    - run: python -m pip install -e ".[docs]"
    - name: Build docs (warnings are errors)
      run: sphinx-build -W --keep-going -b html -d docs/_build/doctrees docs docs/_build/html
    - name: Linkcheck
      if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
      run: sphinx-build -b linkcheck docs docs/_build/linkcheck
      continue-on-error: yes
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: docs-html
        path: docs/_build/html

  build:
    name: Build sdist + wheel
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
         with:
           fetch-depth: 0
       - run: pipx run build
       - run: pipx run twine check --strict dist/*
       - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
         with:
           name: dist
           path: dist/
           if-no-files-found: error



  publish:
    name: Publish to PyPI
    needs: [test, docs, build]
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: { name: pypi, url: https://pypi.org/p/acme-toolkit }
    permissions:
      id-token: write   # trusted publishing -- no API token needed
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - name: Publish
        uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1
        with:
          print-hash: true
          # repository-url: https://test.pypi.org/legacy/
          skip-existing: null

Hi, I'm Lena — a data scientist working on population genetics and, increasingly, on the less glamorous problem of making scientific software that other people can actually install. I'm currently a research software engineer at the [Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics](https://www.sib.swiss/), where I maintain a handful of R and Python packages for variant-calling QC and spend a surprising amount of my week reading other people's `Makefile`s.

Before that I did a PhD at ETH Zürich on selection scans in alpine plant populations, which mostly taught me that the hard part of any analysis is the part that happens *before* the analysis.

Outside of work I climb (badly), bake sourdough (better), and help organise the [Zürich R User Group](https://www.meetup.com/zurich-r-user-group/events/?type=past&utm_source=lena-site&utm_medium=about-page&utm_campaign=2024).

[Get in touch {{< fa envelope >}}](mailto:lena@lenaschroeder.dev){.btn .btn-primary}

**ETH Zürich** | Zürich, Switzerland
PhD in Computational Biology | Sept 2015 – June 2020

**Universität Heidelberg** | Heidelberg, Germany\
MSc in Molecular Biotechnology | Oct 2012 – Aug 2015

**Universität Heidelberg** | Heidelberg, Germany
BSc in Molecular Biotechnology | Oct 2009 – Sept 2012

**Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics** | Research Software Engineer | Oct 2021 – present\
**ETH Zürich**, Plant Ecological Genetics | Postdoc | July 2020 – Sept 2021\
**Roche Diagnostics** | Intern, Biostatistics | summer 2014

:::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Software {{< fa code >}}

- **vcfqc** — fast QC summaries for multi-sample VCFs (R, C++)
- **alpscan** — selection scans for structured populations
    - Python, with a small Rust core
    - used in ~30 papers, which still surprises me
- Contributions to `data.table`, `vcfR` and `scikit-allel`
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Teaching {{< fa chalkboard-user >}}

1. Software Carpentry instructor since 2017
2. *Reproducible research with R* — ETH doctoral course, 2019–2023
3. Occasional workshops on Quarto & `{targets}`
:::

::::

A full list is on [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Xq3bTk0AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao). Highlights:

- Schröder L., Keller I., Widmer A. (2021). Polygenic adaptation along elevational gradients in *Arabis alpina*. [@schroeder2021]
- Schröder L. et al. (2023). vcfqc: interactive quality control for large VCF files. _Bioinformatics_ 39(4). [@schroeder2023]

| 2023 | SciPy (virtual) | Rust inside Python, for scientists | [html](https://lena-schroeder.github.io/talks/scipy2023/) |
| 2022 | Swiss Bioinformatics Day | Variant QC at scale | — |

## Bits and pieces

| Currently reading: *The Book of Why* — J. Pearl
| Currently listening: far too much Bon Iver
| Currently broken: left index finger (climbing, of course)

Contact
-------

Email is best: {{< fa envelope >}} lena@lenaschroeder.dev — I try to reply within a week.
If you're a student looking for a project, please mention which of the packages above you've used.

[^1]: Specifically `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2`, which pushes to the `gh-pages` branch. It took me three attempts to get the `_freeze` directory right.

arguments.content:
---
# CI for the `quiver` workspace (quiver, quiver-core, quiver-derive)
#
#   fmt ────┐
#   clippy ─┼─> test (matrix) ──> coverage
#   deny ───┘
#
# MSRV lives in Cargo.toml (`rust-version`) AND in the matrix below. Keep them in
# sync, `cargo xtask msrv` yells at you otherwise.

name: Rust CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, 'release-*' ]
  workflow_dispatch:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * 0"     # weekly: new nightly + new clippy lints

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  RUSTFLAGS: "-D warnings"
  RUST_BACKTRACE: 1
  CARGO_INCREMENTAL: 0
  CARGO_NET_RETRY:   10
  RUSTUP_MAX_RETRIES:   10

jobs:
  fmt:
    name: rustfmt
    runs-on:   ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly
      with: { components: rustfmt }
    - run: cargo fmt --all -- --check

  clippy:
    name: clippy (${{ matrix.toolchain }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        toolchain: [ stable,beta ]
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master
      with:
        toolchain: ${{ matrix.toolchain }}
        components: clippy
    - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
      with: {key: "clippy-${{ matrix.toolchain }}"}
    - run: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -A clippy::module_name_repetitions


  test:
    name:
      test ${{ matrix.rust }} / ${{ matrix.os }}
      ${{ matrix.target && format('({0})', matrix.target) || '' }}
    needs: [fmt, clippy]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.rust == 'nightly' }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        rust: [stable, beta, nightly, 1.74.0]
            # NB: never write the MSRV as e.g. `msrv: 1.70` -- YAML reads that as the
            # float 1.7 and rustup then tries to install 1.7.0. Ask me how I know.
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
        exclude:
        - rust: beta
          os: macos-latest
        - rust: beta
          os: windows-latest
        - { rust: 1.74.0,  os: windows-latest }
        include:
        - rust: stable
          os: ubuntu-latest
          target: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
          use-cross: true
        - rust: stable
          os: ubuntu-latest
          target: i686-unknown-linux-gnu
          use-cross: true
          features: "--no-default-features"
        - rust: stable
          os: ubuntu-latest
          target: armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf
          use-cross: true
          features: --no-default-features --features std
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master
        with:
          toolchain: ${{ matrix.rust }}
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          key:   ${{ matrix.target }}
          cache-on-failure: true
      - name: Install cross
        if: matrix.use-cross
        uses: taiki-e/install-action@v2
        with: { tool: cross }
      - name: Test
        shell: bash
        run: |
          if [ "${{ matrix.use-cross }}" = "true" ]; then
            cross test --workspace --target ${{ matrix.target }} ${{ matrix.features }}
          else
            cargo test --workspace ${{ matrix.features || '--all-features' }} --no-fail-fast
          fi
      - name: Doctests
        if: matrix.rust == 'stable' && !matrix.target
        run: cargo test --doc --workspace --all-features



  miri:
    name: miri (UB check)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: fmt
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master
        with: { toolchain: nightly, components: "miri, rust-src" }
      - run: cargo miri setup
      - run: cargo miri test -p quiver-core --lib
        env:
            MIRIFLAGS: -Zmiri-strict-provenance -Zmiri-symbolic-alignment-check
            # MIRIFLAGS: -Zmiri-disable-isolation   # once we test the fs module

  cargo-deny:
    name: cargo-deny
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v1
      with:
        command: check bans licenses sources
        arguments: --all-features
        rust-version: "1.74.0"
  # advisories can start failing any day (new RUSTSEC entries) -- don't block PRs on them
    - uses: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v1
      continue-on-error: true
      with:
        command: check advisories

  coverage:
    name: coverage
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'push' || (github.event_name == 'pull_request' && !github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@cargo-llvm-cov
      - name: Collect coverage
        run: cargo llvm-cov --workspace --all-features --lcov --output-path lcov.info
      - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          files: lcov.info
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          fail_ci_if_error: false
          flags: unittests

  semver-checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks-action@v2
        with:
          package: quiver, quiver-core
          feature-group: all-features
          # baseline-rev: v0.9.0

  docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      RUSTDOCFLAGS: --cfg docsrs -D warnings
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly
      - run: cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features
      - name: Private items too
        run: cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items
        env: { RUSTDOCFLAGS: "-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links -D rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links" }

  # branch protection only requires this one
  ci-success:
    name: CI success
    if: always()
    needs: [fmt, clippy, test, miri, cargo-deny, docs]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: exit 0
        if: ${{ !contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') && !contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled') }}
      - run: exit 1
        if: ${{ contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled') }}

          key:   ${{ matrix.target }}
          cache-on-failure: true
      - name: Install cross
        if: matrix.use-cross
        uses: taiki-e/install-action@v2
        with: { tool: cross }
      - name: Test
        shell: bash
        run: |
          if [ "${{ matrix.use-cross }}" = "true" ]; then
            cross test --workspace --target ${{ matrix.target }} ${{ matrix.features }}
          else
            cargo test --workspace ${{ matrix.features || '--all-features' }} --no-fail-fast
          fi
      - name: Doctests
        if: matrix.rust == 'stable' && !matrix.target
        run: cargo test --doc --workspace --all-features



  miri:
    name: miri (UB check)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: fmt
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master
        with: { toolchain: nightly, components: "miri, rust-src" }
      - run: cargo miri setup
      - run: cargo miri test -p quiver-core --lib
        env:
            MIRIFLAGS: -Zmiri-strict-provenance -Zmiri-symbolic-alignment-check
            # MIRIFLAGS: -Zmiri-disable-isolation   # once we test the fs module

  cargo-deny:
    name: cargo-deny
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v1
      with:
        command: check bans licenses sources
        arguments: --all-features
        rust-version: "1.74.0"
  # advisories can start failing any day (new RUSTSEC entries) -- don't block PRs on them
    - uses: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v1
      continue-on-error: true
      with:
        command: check advisories

  coverage:
    name: coverage
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'push' || (github.event_name == 'pull_request' && !github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@cargo-llvm-cov
      - name: Collect coverage
        run: cargo llvm-cov --workspace --all-features --lcov --output-path lcov.info
      - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          files: lcov.info
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          fail_ci_if_error: false
          flags: unittests

  semver-checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks-action@v2
        with:
          package: quiver, quiver-core
          feature-group: all-features
          # baseline-rev: v0.9.0

  docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      RUSTDOCFLAGS: --cfg docsrs -D warnings
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly
      - run: cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features
      - name: Private items too
        run: cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items
        env: { RUSTDOCFLAGS: "-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links -D rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links" }

  # branch protection only requires this one
  ci-success:
    name: CI success
    if: always()
    needs: [fmt, clippy, test, miri, cargo-deny, docs]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: exit 0
        if: ${{ !contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') && !contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled') }}
      - run: exit 1
        if: ${{ contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled') }}

arguments.content: # Contributing to Orbit # [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/acme/orbit/pulls) [![Good first issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/acme/orbit/good%20first%20issue?color=7057ff&label=good%20first%20issues)](https://github.com/acme/orbit/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22) [![DCO](https://img.shields.io/badge/DCO-required-blue)](#developer-certificate-of-origin) First off: thanks for taking the time to contribute! 🎉 Orbit is a community project and we welcome every kind of contribution — bug reports, docs fixes, new executors, dashboard translations, or simply answering questions in [Discussions][discussions]. This document describes how we work. It is a guide, not a law: use your best judgement, and feel free to propose changes to this document in a pull request. **Table of contents** - [Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct) - [I just have a question](#i-just-have-a-question) - [Getting started](#getting-started) - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites) - [Setting up your environment](#setting-up-your-environment) - [Development workflow](#development-workflow) * [Branch naming](#branch-naming) * [Commit messages](#commit-messages) - [Pull request checklist](#pull-request-checklist) - [Running tests](#running-tests) - [Style guide](#style-guide) - [Release process (maintainers)](#release-process-maintainers-only) - [Developer Certificate of Origin](#developer-certificate-of-origin) ## Code of Conduct This project and everyone participating in it is governed by the [Orbit Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By participating you are expected to uphold this code; please report unacceptable behaviour to (only the three members of the moderation team can read that inbox). ## I just have a question > **Note** > Please don't open an issue to ask a question. You'll get faster answers here: * the [FAQ](https://orbit.example.org/docs/faq/) and the [user docs](https://orbit.example.org/docs/latest/?ref=contributing#getting-help) * GitHub [Discussions][discussions] — add the `question` label * `#orbit` on the Acme community Slack ([invite](https://join.slack.com/t/acme-community/shared_invite/zt-2a9xk1f0q-QmV8hR3lZ9pT4yWcE7nB1g)) ## Getting started ### Prerequisites | Tool | Version | Why | |------|---------|-----| | Go | ≥ 1.22 | server, CLI and executors | | Node.js | 20.x LTS | the dashboard in `web/` | | pnpm | 9.x | JS package manager (`corepack enable` installs the pinned version) | | Docker *or* Podman | any recent | integration tests start Postgres 16 + Redis 7 | | `make` | GNU make ≥ 4 | task runner; macOS ships 3.81, which *mostly* works | ### Setting up your environment 1. **Fork** the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork and add the upstream remote: ```bash git clone git@github.com:/orbit.git cd orbit git remote add upstream https://github.com/acme/orbit.git ``` 2. Install the toolchain for your OS: - **macOS** (Homebrew): ```bash brew install go node@20 golangci-lint protobuf corepack enable ``` - **Debian / Ubuntu**: - Go from the official tarball — the distro package is usually too old: ```bash curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.22.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo rm -rf /usr/local/go && sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.22.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz echo 'export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin' >> ~/.profile ``` - Node.js via [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm#installing-and-updating) or the NodeSource packages. - `sudo apt install build-essential protobuf-compiler` - **Fedora**: `sudo dnf install golang nodejs20 protobuf-compiler make` and you're done. - **Windows**: use WSL2 with Ubuntu and follow the Debian steps. Native Windows builds only work for the CLI (`make cli`). 3. Install dependencies and Git hooks: ```bash make bootstrap # go mod download + pnpm install + pre-commit install ``` 4. Start the dev services and the server with live reload: ```bash docker compose -f deploy/dev/compose.yaml up -d make dev ``` The dashboard is served on http://localhost:5173 and proxies `/api` to the Go server on `:8080`. 5. Make sure everything is green before you start hacking: `make test`. ## Development workflow We use a simple trunk-based flow: `main` is always releasable, and feature work happens on short-lived branches in your fork. Rebase, don't merge `main` into your branch. ### Branch naming Prefix | Use for | Example --- | --- | --- `feat/` | new features | `feat/cron-timezones` `fix/` | bug fixes, ideally with the issue number | `fix/1287-retry-backoff-overflow` `docs/` | documentation only | `docs/executor-tutorial` `chore/` | tooling, dependencies, CI | `chore/bump-golangci-lint` `exp/` | experiments you don't expect to merge | `exp/wasm-executor` ### Commit messages We follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#specification) because both the changelog and the version bump are generated from the history[^release-please]. The format is ```text (): ``` Some examples from the log: ``` feat(scheduler): support IANA time zones in cron expressions fix(api): return 404 instead of 500 for unknown job IDs Closes #1291 refactor(executor/docker)!: drop support for Docker API < 1.41 BREAKING CHANGE: Docker Engine 20.10 or newer is now required. ``` | Type | Changelog section | Version bump | |:-----|:------------------|-------------:| | `feat` | Features | minor | | `fix` | Bug Fixes | patch | | `perf` | Performance Improvements | patch | | `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `ci`, `refactor`, `build` | *(not shown)* | — | | any type with `!`, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer | ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES | **major** | ## Pull request checklist Before you mark your PR as _ready for review_, please check that: - [ ] the PR targets `main` and is rebased on the latest `upstream/main` - [ ] `make lint test` passes locally - [ ] new behaviour is covered by tests - [ ] unit tests for pure logic (`*_test.go` next to the code) - [ ] an integration test under `test/integration/` if it touches the database or an executor - [ ] user-facing changes are documented in `docs/` — or you opened a follow-up issue - [ ] all commits follow the convention above and are signed off (`git commit -s`) - [x] you've read this guide 😉 Small PRs get reviewed __much__ faster. If your change is bigger than ~400 lines, open a [design discussion][discussions] first so nobody wastes a weekend. ## Running tests `make test` : Go unit tests (`go test ./... -race -count=1`) plus the dashboard's Vitest suite. About two minutes on a laptop. `make test-integration` : Starts Postgres and Redis with Docker Compose and runs every test behind the `integration` build tag. Set `ORBIT_TEST_KEEP_CONTAINERS=1` to leave the containers running afterwards, which is handy with `psql`. `make e2e` : Playwright tests against the full stack. Run `pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps` once beforehand. `go test ./internal/scheduler -run 'TestCron/timezone' -v` : Runs a single test. Much faster than the make targets while iterating. ## Style guide * **Go** * Formatting by `gofumpt` + `goimports`, enforced through `golangci-lint` (see `.golangci.yml`). * Wrap errors with `fmt.Errorf("loading job %q: %w", id, err)`; don't add `pkg/errors`. * Anything under `internal/` may change at any time. Anything under `pkg/` is public API: + exported identifiers need doc comments, + breaking it needs a `!` commit and a note in `docs/upgrading.md`. * **TypeScript / React** * ESLint + Prettier via `pnpm lint` — please don't fight the formatter. * Function components and hooks only; no new class components. * Use the design-system components in `web/src/ui/` rather than raw `

arguments.content:
---
title: "Getting started with tidyfoo"
author: "Priya Raman and Tomás Ferreira"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output:
  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with tidyfoo}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: none
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(tidyfoo)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

Survey platforms such as Qualtrics, LimeSurvey and SoSci Survey all export data in slightly different shapes: some put the question text in a second header row, some encode "don't know" as `-99`, others as `999` or as an empty string, and almost all of them produce column names like `Q12_3_TEXT` that mean nothing outside the original questionnaire. tidyfoo gives you a small set of verbs that turn such an export into a tidy data frame with one row per respondent, consistent column names, proper factors for Likert items and a codebook you can hand to your co-authors, i.e. the boring 80% of every survey project that nobody wants to write twice.

This vignette walks through a complete, if small, example. It assumes you know the basics of dplyr (e.g. `filter()`, `mutate()` and the pipe); if not, the [data transformation chapter of R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#introduction) is a good place to start. Everything below runs in a few seconds on the example data that ships with the package, so feel free to copy the code into a script and follow along.

<!-- TODO (TF): add the speeders plot once the ggplot2 3.5 release is on CRAN; the current version needs the dev branch -->

## The example data

tidyfoo ships with a small, anonymised extract from a well-being survey run by Dr. Amara Okonkwo's group at the University of Leeds in 2023 (n = 412, 57 columns). The raw Qualtrics export is included as-is, warts and all, so that you can see exactly what each step does to it. Respondents gave informed consent for the anonymised data to be shared for teaching purposes; free-text answers were removed beforehand, as were IP addresses and the approx. location fields that Qualtrics adds by default.

```{r}
path <- tf_example("wellbeing_2023.csv")
raw <- tf_read(path, platform = "qualtrics")
dim(raw)
names(raw)[1:12]
```

`tf_read()` already does a few things for you: it drops the second and third header rows that Qualtrics adds (question text and import IDs), stores the question text as a `label` attribute on each column, and converts the `StartDate`/`EndDate` columns to `POSIXct` in the time zone recorded in the file. It does *not* rename anything or touch the values yet, because those decisions depend on your questionnaire and we would rather you made them explicitly.


## The verbs ##

The package is built around a handful of verbs that each do one thing:

- `tf_clean_names()` --- turns `Q12_3_TEXT` into something like `q12_3_text`, or, if you supply a lookup table, into a meaningful name such as `sleep_quality_text`.
- `tf_recode_missing()` --- converts platform-specific missing codes (`-99`, `-77`, `999`, `""`) to `NA`, optionally keeping the reason in a separate column.
- `tf_recode_likert()` --- turns item responses into ordered factors with consistent levels.
    - Works on labels ("Strongly agree") as well as on numeric codes.
    - Reverse-coded items are handled via `reverse = c(...)`; no more `6 - x` scattered across your scripts.
- `tf_score()` --- computes scale scores (mean or sum) with a minimum-valid-items rule.
- `tf_codebook()` --- produces a codebook as a data frame, or as HTML/Word via `tf_codebook_render()`.

* `tf_check()` --- runs a battery of plausibility checks (straight-lining, speeders, out-of-range values) and returns a tidy report.

Most verbs take a data frame as their first argument and return a data frame, so they compose with the pipe. The exceptions are `tf_labels()` and `tf_codebook()`, which return a tibble *describing* your data rather than the data itself.

## A typical workflow

In practice we nearly always go through the same steps, in this order:

1. Read the export with `tf_read()` and look at the labels (`tf_labels(raw)`).
1. Clean the names. For anything you will actually analyse, use a lookup table rather than the automatic names: the automatic names are fine for exploration, but they change whenever the questionnaire changes, e.g. when an item is added in a later wave or the platform renumbers the blocks.
1. Recode missing values.
1. Recode Likert items and compute scale scores.
1. Run `tf_check()` and decide, *before* looking at the outcomes, which respondents to exclude. Write that decision down (a pre-registration is ideal, a comment in the script is the bare minimum).
1. Write the codebook.

Steps 2--4 look like this:

```{r}
lookup <- tf_example_lookup("wellbeing_2023")
head(lookup, 4)

clean <- raw |>
  tf_clean_names(lookup = lookup) |>
  tf_recode_missing(codes = c(-99, -77)) |>
  tf_recode_likert(
    starts_with("wemwbs_"),
    levels = c("None of the time", "Rarely", "Some of the time", "Often", "All of the time")
  ) |>
  tf_score(wemwbs_total = starts_with("wemwbs_"), fun = "sum", min_valid = 12)

clean |>
  select(respondent_id, age_group, wemwbs_total) |>
  head()
```

The WEMWBS has 14 items scored 1--5, so totals range from 14 to 70; `min_valid = 12` means that a respondent needs at least 12 valid items for a total to be computed, and the remaining items are prorated.[^prorate] If you would rather not prorate, set `prorate = FALSE` and any respondent with a missing item gets `NA`. Which option is better depends on the instrument and on why the items are missing, cf. the discussion in Mazza et al. (2015) and the scoring guidance by Tennant et al. (2007), and we deliberately do not pick a default that hides the choice from you.

## Checking data quality

`tf_check()` never removes anything by itself. It flags, and you decide:

```{r}
report <- tf_check(clean, duration = "duration_sec", items = starts_with("wemwbs_"))
report
```

When a check cannot be run, you get an informative error rather than a silent `NA`:

```{r, error = TRUE}
tf_check(clean, duration = "time_taken")
```

| Check | Default threshold | Argument | Notes |
|:------|------------------:|:---------|:------|
| Speeders | < 1/3 of median duration | `speed_ratio` | Uses `duration_sec` unless you say otherwise |
| Straight-lining | ≥ 10 identical consecutive answers | `max_run` | Only within the item set you pass to `items` |
| Out of range | outside the declared levels | --- | Needs the Likert items recoded first |
|Duplicates|identical `ResponseId`, or IP + user agent|`dup_keys`|IP addresses are hashed by `tf_read()` by default|

## Codebooks

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tf_codebook(clean) |>
  tf_codebook_render("codebook.docx", title = "Well-being survey 2023 — codebook")
```

```{r setup}

This vignette walks through a complete, if small, example. ## The example data

tidyfoo ships with a small, anonymised extract from a well-being survey run by Dr. Amara Okonkwo's group at the University of Leeds in 2023 (n = 412, 57 columns). The raw Qualtrics export is included as-is, warts and all, so that you can see exactly what each step does to it. Respondents gave informed consent for the anonymised data to be shared for teaching purposes; free-text answers were removed beforehand, as were IP addresses and the approx. location fields that Qualtrics adds by default.

```{r}
path <- tf_example("wellbeing_2023.csv")
raw <- tf_read(path, platform = "qualtrics")
dim(raw)
names(raw)[1:12]
```

`tf_read()` already does a few things for you: it drops the second and third header rows that Qualtrics adds (question text and import IDs), stores the question text as a `label` attribute on each column, and converts the `StartDate`/`EndDate` columns to `POSIXct` in the time zone recorded in the file. It does *not* rename anything or touch the values yet, because those decisions depend on your questionnaire and we would rather you made them explicitly.


## The verbs ##

The package is built around a handful of verbs that each do one thing:

- `tf_clean_names()` --- turns `Q12_3_TEXT` into something like `q12_3_text`, or, if you supply a lookup table, into a meaningful name such as `sleep_quality_text`.
- `tf_recode_missing()` --- converts platform-specific missing codes (`-99`, `-77`, `999`, `""`) to `NA`, optionally keeping the reason in a separate column.
- `tf_recode_likert()` --- turns item responses into ordered factors with consistent levels.
    - Works on labels ("Strongly agree") as well as on numeric codes.
    - Reverse-coded items are handled via `reverse = c(...)`; no more `6 - x` scattered across your scripts.
- `tf_score()` --- computes scale scores (mean or sum) with a minimum-valid-items rule.
- `tf_codebook()` --- produces a codebook as a data frame, or as HTML/Word via `tf_codebook_render()`.

* `tf_check()` --- runs a battery of plausibility checks (straight-lining, speeders, out-of-range values) and returns a tidy report.

Most verbs take a data frame as their first argument and return a data frame, so they compose with the pipe. The exceptions are `tf_labels()` and `tf_codebook()`, which return a tibble *describing* your data rather than the data itself.

## A typical workflow

In practice we nearly always go through the same steps, in this order:

1. Read the export with `tf_read()` and look at the labels (`tf_labels(raw)`).
1. Clean the names. For anything you will actually analyse, use a lookup table rather than the automatic names: the automatic names are fine for exploration, but they change whenever the questionnaire changes, e.g. when an item is added in a later wave or the platform renumbers the blocks.
1. Recode missing values.
1. Recode Likert items and compute scale scores.
1. Run `tf_check()` and decide, *before* looking at the outcomes, which respondents to exclude. Write that decision down (a pre-registration is ideal, a comment in the script is the bare minimum).
1. Write the codebook.

```{r}

head(lookup, 4)

  tf_clean_names(lookup = lookup) |>
  tf_recode_missing(codes = c(-99, -77)) |>
  tf_recode_likert(
    starts_with("wemwbs_"),
    levels = c("None of the time", "Rarely", "Some of the time", "Often", "All of the time")
  ) |>
  tf_score(wemwbs_total = starts_with("wemwbs_"), fun = "sum", min_valid = 12)

  select(respondent_id, age_group, wemwbs_total) |>
  head()
```

The WEMWBS has 14 items scored 1--5, so totals range from 14 to 70; `min_valid = 12` means that a respondent needs at least 12 valid items for a total to be computed, and the remaining items are prorated.[^prorate] If you would rather not prorate, set `prorate = FALSE` and any respondent with a missing item gets `NA`. (2007), and we deliberately do not pick a default that hides the choice from you.

## Checking data quality

`tf_check()` never removes anything by itself. It flags, and you decide:

```{r}
report <- tf_check(clean, duration = "duration_sec", items = starts_with("wemwbs_"))
report
```

When a check cannot be run, you get an informative error rather than a silent `NA`:

```{r, error = TRUE}

# RFC 0042: Async plugin hooks

- Feature Name: `async_plugins`
- Start Date: 2024-02-12
- RFC PR: [acme/rfcs#42](https://github.com/acme/rfcs/pull/42)
- Tracking Issue: [acme/forge#3817](https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/3817)
- Authors: Priya Raman (@priyar), Jonas Weber (@jweber)
- Status: **Accepted** (FCP ended 2024-03-29)

## Summary

Allow Forge plugins to implement their hooks as `async` functions, both in Rust
and in TypeScript, so that plugins can perform I/O (network requests, reading
large files, talking to a language server) without blocking the build
scheduler. Existing synchronous plugins keep working unchanged.

## Motivation

Today every hook runs on one of the scheduler's worker threads and is expected
to return quickly. In practice, plugins do all sorts of slow things in hooks:

* fetching remote modules (`https://` imports in the `remote-imports` plugin),
* calling out to `esbuild` or `swc` subprocesses,
* querying a database for content (the CMS plugins), and
* waiting for a TypeScript language service to type-check a file.

When a hook blocks, the worker thread is gone for that time. With the default
pool of `num_cpus` workers, four slow fetches on a laptop are enough to stall
the whole build. We have seen this in the wild repeatedly — see [#2950],
[#3101] and the infamous "build hangs on airplane wifi" thread.[^wifi]

Plugin authors currently work around it in one of three ways, all of them bad:

1. **Spawning their own runtime.** Several plugins create a private Tokio
   runtime inside the hook and `block_on` a future:

   ```rust
   fn on_load(&self, ctx: &mut LoadContext) -> Result<Option<Module>> {
       let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new()?; // a new runtime. per call.
       rt.block_on(self.fetch(ctx.url()))
   }
   ```

   This still blocks the worker, creates threads on every call, and panics if
   the hook happens to be invoked from inside an existing runtime.

2. **Pre-fetching everything in `on_start`.** Works for small sites, falls
   over for anything with more than a few hundred remote resources, and makes
   incremental rebuilds pointless.

3. **Giving up**, and telling users to run a separate script before the build.

None of these compose. Two plugins that each spin up a runtime will happily
fight over the same file descriptors, and nobody can reason about the result.

## Guide-level explanation

With this RFC, a Rust plugin can implement hooks as `async fn`:

```rust
use forge_plugin::prelude::*;

pub struct RemoteImports {
    client: reqwest::Client,
}

impl Plugin for RemoteImports {
    async fn on_load(&self, ctx: &mut LoadContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Module>> {
        if !ctx.url().starts_with("https://") {
            return Ok(None);
        }
        let body = self.client.get(ctx.url()).send().await?.text().await?;
        Ok(Some(Module::js(body)))
    }
}
```

and a TypeScript plugin simply returns a promise:

```ts
import { definePlugin } from "@forge/plugin";

export default definePlugin({
  name: "cms-content",
  async onLoad(ctx) {
    if (!ctx.id.startsWith("cms:")) return null;
    const entry = await cms.getEntry(ctx.id.slice(4));
    return { code: `export default ${JSON.stringify(entry)}`, loader: "js" };
  },
});
```

Nothing else changes for plugin authors. Sync hooks keep working, and a plugin
may mix sync and async hooks freely.

## Reference-level explanation

### Hook signatures

All hook methods on the `Plugin` trait become `async fn`s, using native
async-fn-in-trait (stable since Rust 1.75, which is already our MSRV). A
blanket adapter, `SyncPlugin`, keeps the old signatures compiling:

```rust
pub trait Plugin: Send + Sync + 'static {
    async fn on_start(&self, _ctx: &mut StartContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
    async fn on_resolve(&self, _ctx: &mut ResolveContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Resolved>> { Ok(None) }
    async fn on_load(&self, _ctx: &mut LoadContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Module>> { Ok(None) }
    async fn on_end(&self, _ctx: &mut EndContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}
```

### Scheduling

1. The scheduler moves from a fixed thread pool to a multi-threaded Tokio
   runtime.

   Sync hooks are run through `spawn_blocking`, so a slow sync hook occupies a
   blocking thread rather than a core worker. The blocking pool is capped at
   `max(64, 4 * num_cpus)` threads; the cap is configurable as
   `scheduler.blocking_threads`.

2. Async hooks are polled on the core workers.

   A hook that blocks *inside* an `async fn` (e.g. `std::fs::read` on a slow
   network drive) will still stall a worker. In debug builds we detect polls
   that take longer than 50 ms and log a warning that names the plugin and
   the hook.

3. Hook ordering is unchanged: for each module, `on_resolve` hooks run in
   plugin order until one returns `Some`, then `on_load` hooks do the same.

   Different modules are processed concurrently, as they are today.

### Cancellation

When a build is cancelled (a file changes during `forge dev`, or the user presses <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>), outstanding hook
futures are dropped. Plugins must therefore be cancel-safe at every `.await` point. This is the single biggest
behavioural change in this RFC, and it gets its own section in the plugin author guide.

### TypeScript plugins

The JS host already runs an event loop, but today it blocks on each promise
before returning to Rust. After this change promises are bridged to Rust
futures via `forge_js::PromiseFuture`, so up to `js.max_inflight` (default: 32)
hook calls can be pending per isolate.

## Drawbacks

- A more complex scheduler, which is harder to debug.
    - Stack traces through async code are worse, particularly across the JS bridge.
    - `tokio-console` support helps, but it is opt-in.
- Cancel-safety is a new obligation for plugin authors, and getting it wrong
  produces bugs that are rare and hard to reproduce.
- Compile times for `forge-core` grow by roughly 8% (measured on CI, see the
  [benchmark gist](https://gist.github.com/priyar/4b1f0c2d7e9a8b3c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4#file-compile-times-md)).

## Rationale and alternatives

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|:-------|:-----|:-----|:-------:|
| **A. Native async hooks** (this RFC) | No workarounds needed; same model for Rust and TS | Scheduler rewrite; cancel-safety | ✅ |
| B. Bigger thread pool | Trivial to implement | Doesn't fix the problem, only moves the cliff | ❌ |
| C. `#[async_trait]` macro | Works on older compilers | Boxes every future, worse error messages, and our MSRV is 1.75 anyway | ❌ |
| D. Callback / continuation API | No async runtime in core | Awful ergonomics (see Prior art) | ❌ |
| E. Separate "fetch" phase before the build | Simple mental model | Breaks incremental builds; doesn't help the LSP use case | ❌ |

We considered shipping B as a stop-gap. It was rejected in the design meeting
on 2024-02-28 because it would make the migration *look* less urgent without
actually fixing anything.

## Prior art

* Rollup and Vite: plugin hooks may return promises, and hooks for different
  modules run concurrently. This RFC is heavily inspired by that model.
* esbuild: `onLoad`/`onResolve` callbacks in JS are async; Go plugins are
  synchronous but run on goroutines, so blocking is cheap.
* Parcel 2: plugins are async throughout and run in worker farms.
* Bazel: no in-process plugins at all; everything is a separate action, which
  sidesteps the problem at a large cost in flexibility.

## Unresolved questions

1. Should `on_end` hooks be allowed to run concurrently with each other? Some
   plugins (`sitemap`, `rss`) write files that others (`compress`) read.
2. What is the right default for `js.max_inflight`? 32 is an educated guess.
3. Do we expose the Tokio runtime handle to plugins, or only a narrow
   `forge_plugin::spawn` API? The latter keeps our options open if we ever
   want to swap the runtime.

## Future possibilities

- Streaming `on_load` results, so that large generated modules don't have to be
  buffered in memory.
- A `Plugin::on_watch` hook for plugins that watch external resources (e.g. a
  CMS webhook) and want to trigger rebuilds.
- Reusing the same machinery for the dev server's HMR pipeline.

[^wifi]: [acme/forge discussion #2777](https://github.com/acme/forge/discussions/2777): a 40-minute
    build that turned out to be one plugin retrying DNS lookups with a 30-second timeout, one after another.

[#2950]: https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/2950
[#3101]: https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/3101 "Build stalls when the remote-imports plugin is enabled"

* esbuild: `onLoad`/`onResolve` callbacks in JS are async; Go plugins are
  synchronous but run on goroutines, so blocking is cheap.
* Parcel 2: plugins are async throughout and run in worker farms.
* Bazel: no in-process plugins at all; everything is a separate action, which
  sidesteps the problem at a large cost in flexibility.

## Unresolved questions

1. Should `on_end` hooks be allowed to run concurrently with each other? Some
   plugins (`sitemap`, `rss`) write files that others (`compress`) read.
2. What is the right default for `js.max_inflight`? 32 is an educated guess.
3. Do we expose the Tokio runtime handle to plugins, or only a narrow
   `forge_plugin::spawn` API? The latter keeps our options open if we ever
   want to swap the runtime.

## Future possibilities

- Streaming `on_load` results, so that large generated modules don't have to be
  buffered in memory.
- A `Plugin::on_watch` hook for plugins that watch external resources (e.g. a
  CMS webhook) and want to trigger rebuilds.
- Reusing the same machinery for the dev server's HMR pipeline.

[#3101]: https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/3101 "Build stalls when the remote-imports plugin is enabled"

# Prometheus alerting & recording rules — platform team
# Loaded via prometheus.yml:  rule_files: ["/etc/prometheus/rules/*.yml"]
# Lint before committing:     promtool check rules prometheus-rules.yml
#
# Severity convention: critical = pages on-call | warning = Slack #alerts-platform | info = dashboards only
---
groups:

  - name: node.rules
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - alert: HostOutOfMemory
        expr: node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100 < 10
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: Host out of memory (instance {{ $labels.instance }})
          description: "Node memory is filling up (< 10% left)\n  VALUE = {{ $value }}\n  LABELS = {{ $labels }}"
          runbook_url: https://runbooks.acme.example.com/platform/alerts/node/host-out-of-memory#first-response-checklist

      - alert: HostOutOfDiskSpace
        expr: |
          (
            node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype!~"tmpfs|overlay|squashfs"} * 100
              / node_filesystem_size_bytes{fstype!~"tmpfs|overlay|squashfs"} < 10
          )
          and on(instance, device, mountpoint)
            node_filesystem_readonly{fstype!~"tmpfs|overlay|squashfs"} == 0
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: critical,team: platform }
        annotations:
          summary: "Host out of disk space (instance {{ $labels.instance }})"
          description: |-
            Disk {{ $labels.device }} mounted on {{ $labels.mountpoint }} is almost full
            ({{ printf "%.2f" $value }}% left).
          runbook_url: https://runbooks.acme.example.com/platform/alerts/node/host-out-of-disk-space

      - alert: HostDiskWillFillIn24Hours
        expr: >-
          predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype!~"tmpfs|overlay"}[6h], 24 * 3600) < 0
          and on(instance, device, mountpoint) node_filesystem_readonly == 0
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: Disk on {{ $labels.instance }} will fill up within 24h
          description: Filesystem {{ $labels.mountpoint }} on {{ $labels.instance }} is predicted to run out of space within the next 24 hours at the current write rate.

      - alert: HostHighCpuLoad
        expr: |
          (
            1 - avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]))
          ) * on(instance) group_left(nodename) node_uname_info > 0.9
        for: 10m
        keep_firing_for: 5m
        labels:
          severity:   warning
        annotations:
          summary: High CPU load on {{ $labels.nodename }}
          description: 'CPU usage is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} on {{ $labels.instance }} for more than 10 minutes.'

      # - alert: HostClockSkew          # disabled: chrony exporter is not rolled out everywhere yet (#877)
      #   expr: abs(node_timex_offset_seconds) > 0.05
      #   for: 10m


  - name: kubernetes.rules
    rules:
    - alert: KubePodCrashLooping
      expr: max_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{reason="CrashLoopBackOff", job="kube-state-metrics"}[5m]) >= 1
      for: 15m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: "Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} ({{ $labels.container }}) is crash looping"
        description: Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} has been in CrashLoopBackOff for more than 15 minutes.
        runbook_url: https://runbooks.prometheus-operator.dev/runbooks/kubernetes/kubepodcrashlooping
    - alert: KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch
      expr: |
        (
          kube_deployment_spec_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}
            >
          kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{job="kube-state-metrics"}
        ) and (
          changes(kube_deployment_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[10m]) == 0
        )
        unless on(namespace, deployment) kube_deployment_spec_paused == 1
      for: 15m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: Deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} replicas mismatch
    - alert: KubeContainerOOMKilled
      expr: >-
        (kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total - kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total offset 10m >= 1)
        and ignoring (reason)
        min_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}[10m]) == 1
      for: 0m
      labels:
        severity: info
      annotations:
        summary: Container {{ $labels.container }} in {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} was OOMKilled


  - name: blackbox.rules
    rules:
      - alert: ProbeFailed
        expr: probe_success == 0
        for: 3m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          page: "true"
        annotations:
          summary: Probe failed for {{ $labels.instance }}
          description: "Blackbox probe {{ $labels.job }} against {{ $labels.instance }} has been failing for 3 minutes. Check the target, DNS and the TLS certificate before escalating."
      - alert: SslCertificateExpiresSoon
        expr: (probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry - time()) / 86400 < 14
        for: 1h
        labels: {severity: warning}
        annotations:
          summary: SSL certificate for {{ $labels.instance }} expires in less than 14 days
          description: |
            The certificate presented by {{ $labels.instance }} expires in {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} days.
            cert-manager should have renewed it already — check `kubectl get certificate -A`.
      - alert: ProbeSlowerThanLastWeek
        expr: avg_over_time(probe_duration_seconds[5m]) > 1
           and
           avg_over_time(probe_duration_seconds[5m] offset 1w) < 0.5
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: info
        annotations:
          summary: Probe {{ $labels.instance }} is much slower than last week

    # postgres_exporter >= 0.15 metric names
  - name: postgres.rules
    rules:
       - alert: PostgresqlDown
         expr: pg_up == 0
         for: 1m
         labels:
            severity: critical
            team: db
         annotations:
            summary: Postgresql down (instance {{ $labels.instance }})
       - alert: PostgresqlTooManyConnections
         expr: |
            sum by (instance, datname) (pg_stat_activity_count{datname!~"template.*|postgres"})
              > on(instance) group_left()
            pg_settings_max_connections * 0.8
         for: 2m
         labels:
            severity: warning
            team: db
         annotations:
            summary: "PostgreSQL instance {{ $labels.instance }} has too many connections (> 80%)"
       - alert: PostgresqlReplicationLag
         expr: pg_replication_lag_seconds > 30 and on(instance) pg_replication_is_replica == 1
         for: 5m
         labels: { severity: warning, team: db }
         annotations:
            summary: Replication lag on {{ $labels.instance }} is {{ humanizeDuration $value }}
            runbook_url: "https://runbooks.acme.example.com/db/alerts/postgresql-replication-lag?utm_source=alertmanager&utm_medium=slack"
       # - alert: PostgresqlDeadLocks   # too noisy during the nightly batch, revisit
       #   expr: increase(pg_stat_database_deadlocks{datname!~"template.*|postgres"}[1m]) > 5


  - name: slo.api.rules
    interval: 1m
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
      - record: job:http_requests_errors:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate5m
        expr: job:http_requests_errors:rate5m / job:http_requests:rate5m
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate30m
        expr: |-
          sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[30m]))
          /
          sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[30m]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate1h
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[1h]))
      - record: job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate6h
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[6h])) / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[6h]))

      # multi-window, multi-burn-rate (SRE workbook ch. 5); 99.9% target => error budget 0.001
      - alert: ErrorBudgetBurn
        expr: |
          (
              job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate1h{job="api"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
            and
              job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate5m{job="api"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
          )
          or
          (
              job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate6h{job="api"} > (6 * 0.001)
            and
              job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate30m{job="api"} > (6 * 0.001)
          )
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          slo: api-availability
        annotations:
          summary: API is burning its error budget too fast
          description: >
            The api job is consuming the 30-day error budget at more than 6x the sustainable rate.
            At this rate the whole budget is gone in less than 5 days.
          dashboard: https://grafana.acme.example.com/d/slo-api/api-slo?orgId=1&var-job=api&from=now-6h&to=now
...

arguments.content:
# Dependabot configuration
# https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/dependabot-version-updates/configuration-options-for-the-dependabot.yml-file
#
# Grouping policy (agreed in #1452):
#   * minor + patch updates for one ecosystem land in ONE weekly PR per group
#   * majors always get their own PR so they can be reviewed / tested separately
#   * security updates ignore all of this and are opened immediately

version: 2

registries:
  npm-github:
    type: npm-registry
    url: https://npm.pkg.github.com
    token: ${{secrets.DEPENDABOT_NPM_TOKEN}}
    replaces-base: true
  docker-hub:
    type: docker-registry
    url: registry.hub.docker.com
    username: acme-bot
    password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
  python-internal:
      type: python-index
      url: https://pypi.acme.example.com/simple/
      username: dependabot
      password: "${{ secrets.INTERNAL_PYPI_PASSWORD }}"


updates:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- JS (web + admin)
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: monday
      time: "06:00"
      timezone: Europe/Berlin
    open-pull-requests-limit: 10
    registries: [ npm-github ]
    versioning-strategy: increase
    groups:
      eslint:
        patterns:
          - "eslint"
          - "eslint-*"
          - "@typescript-eslint/*"
      types:
        patterns: ["@types/*"]
        update-types: [minor, patch]
      aws-sdk:
        patterns: [ "@aws-sdk/*" ]
      dev-dependencies:
        dependency-type: development
        update-types: [
            "minor",
            "patch"
          ]
        exclude-patterns:
        - "typescript"
        - "@types/*"
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: "react"
        versions: [ ">=19.0.0" ]
      - dependency-name: "react-dom"
        versions: [ ">=19.0.0" ]       # must move together with react, see #1501
      - dependency-name: "@types/node"
        update-types: ["version-update:semver-major"]
      -   dependency-name: "typescript"
          update-types:
            - "version-update:semver-major"
            - "version-update:semver-minor"
    commit-message:
      prefix: "deps"
      prefix-development: "deps(dev)"
      include: scope
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - "javascript"
    reviewers:
      - "acme/frontend"
    assignees: [ octocat ]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- python API
  - package-ecosystem: pip
    directory: /services/api
    registries:
      - python-internal
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
      day: "wednesday"
      time: '04:30'
    insecure-external-code-execution: deny
    allow:
    - dependency-type: direct
    - dependency-name: "django*"
      dependency-type: all
    groups:
      django:
        patterns: [django, "django-*", djangorestframework]
      pytest:
        patterns: [ pytest,"pytest-*", coverage ]
    ignore:
       # celery 6 drops py3.8 and we still run workers on the old AMI (INFRA-77)
      - dependency-name: celery
        versions: ["6.x"]
    labels: [dependencies, python]
    rebase-strategy: disabled
    milestone: ~

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- containers
  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directories: ["/", "/services/*"]
    registries:
    - docker-hub
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: "node"
        # only even-numbered (LTS) majors
        versions: ["21.x", "23.x"]
      - dependency-name: postgres
        update-types: [ "version-update:semver-major" ]

  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
       interval: monthly
       time: 12:30
    groups: { actions: { patterns: ['*'] } }
    commit-message: {prefix: ci}


  - package-ecosystem: terraform
    directory: /infra/terraform
    schedule: { interval: weekly, day: thursday }
    target-branch: develop
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - terraform
    open-pull-requests-limit: 0     # security updates only (0 disables version updates)

  - package-ecosystem: gomod
    directory: /tools/acmectl
    vendor: yes
    schedule:
      interval: daily
      time: "09:00"
    groups:
      golang-x:
        patterns:
          - "golang.org/x/*"
      otel:
        patterns: ["go.opentelemetry.io/*"]
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go
        # v1 is in maintenance mode; the migration to v2 is tracked in #1620
        update-types: ["version-update:semver-major", 'version-update:semver-minor']
    pull-request-branch-name:
      separator: "-"
    labels:
    - dependencies
    - go

    type: npm-registry
    url: https://npm.pkg.github.com
    token: ${{secrets.DEPENDABOT_NPM_TOKEN}}
    replaces-base: true
  docker-hub:
    type: docker-registry
    url: registry.hub.docker.com
    username: acme-bot
    password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
  python-internal:
      type: python-index
      url: https://pypi.acme.example.com/simple/
      username: dependabot
      password: "${{ secrets.INTERNAL_PYPI_PASSWORD }}"


updates:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- JS (web + admin)
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
      day: monday
      time: "06:00"
      timezone: Europe/Berlin
    open-pull-requests-limit: 10
    registries: [ npm-github ]
    versioning-strategy: increase
    groups:
      eslint:
        patterns:
          - "eslint"
          - "eslint-*"
          - "@typescript-eslint/*"
      types:
        patterns: ["@types/*"]
        update-types: [minor, patch]
      aws-sdk:
        patterns: [ "@aws-sdk/*" ]
      dev-dependencies:
        dependency-type: development
        update-types: [
            "minor",
            "patch"
          ]
        exclude-patterns:
        - "typescript"
        - "@types/*"
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: "react"
        versions: [ ">=19.0.0" ]
      - dependency-name: "react-dom"
        versions: [ ">=19.0.0" ]       # must move together with react, see #1501
      - dependency-name: "@types/node"
        update-types: ["version-update:semver-major"]
      -   dependency-name: "typescript"
          update-types:
            - "version-update:semver-major"
            - "version-update:semver-minor"
    commit-message:
      prefix: "deps"
      prefix-development: "deps(dev)"
      include: scope
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - "javascript"
    reviewers:
      - "acme/frontend"
    assignees: [ octocat ]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- python API
  - package-ecosystem: pip
    directory: /services/api
    registries:
      - python-internal
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
      day: "wednesday"
      time: '04:30'
    insecure-external-code-execution: deny
    allow:
    - dependency-type: direct
    - dependency-name: "django*"
      dependency-type: all
    groups:
      django:
        patterns: [django, "django-*", djangorestframework]
      pytest:
        patterns: [ pytest,"pytest-*", coverage ]
    ignore:
       # celery 6 drops py3.8 and we still run workers on the old AMI (INFRA-77)
      - dependency-name: celery
        versions: ["6.x"]
    labels: [dependencies, python]
    rebase-strategy: disabled
    milestone: ~

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- containers
  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directories: ["/", "/services/*"]
    registries:
    - docker-hub
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: "node"
        # only even-numbered (LTS) majors
        versions: ["21.x", "23.x"]
      - dependency-name: postgres
        update-types: [ "version-update:semver-major" ]

  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
       interval: monthly
       time: 12:30
    groups: { actions: { patterns: ['*'] } }
    commit-message: {prefix: ci}


  - package-ecosystem: terraform
    directory: /infra/terraform
    schedule: { interval: weekly, day: thursday }
    target-branch: develop
    labels:
      - dependencies
      - terraform
    open-pull-requests-limit: 0     # security updates only (0 disables version updates)

  - package-ecosystem: gomod
    directory: /tools/acmectl
    vendor: yes
    schedule:
      interval: daily
      time: "09:00"
    groups:
      golang-x:
        patterns:
          - "golang.org/x/*"
      otel:
        patterns: ["go.opentelemetry.io/*"]
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go
        # v1 is in maintenance mode; the migration to v2 is tracked in #1620
        update-types: ["version-update:semver-major", 'version-update:semver-minor']
    pull-request-branch-name:
      separator: "-"
    labels:
    - dependencies
    - go

---
title: "Mapping topsoil organic carbon stocks in Mediterranean agroecosystems with Sentinel-2 time series and random forests"
short-title: "Topsoil SOC mapping with Sentinel-2"
author:
  - name: Elena Martínez-Ruiz
    email: elena.martinez@uco.example.es
    orcid: 0000-0001-7362-4419
    corresponding: true
    affiliations:
      - ref: uni1
      - ref: inst2
  - name: Johannes K. Weber
    orcid: 0000-0002-3150-8812
    affiliations:
      - ref: inst2
  - name: Aïcha Benali
    affiliations:
      - ref: uni1
affiliations:
  - id: uni1
    name: Universidad de Córdoba
    department: Departamento de Agronomía
    city: Córdoba
    country: Spain
  - id: inst2
    name: Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF)
    city: Müncheberg
    country: Germany
abstract: |
  Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a key indicator of soil health, yet
  field-scale maps for Mediterranean croplands remain scarce. We combined
  412 topsoil samples (0–30 cm) collected in Andalusia between 2019 and
  2022 with multi-temporal Sentinel-2 composites, terrain attributes and
  legacy soil maps to predict SOC stocks using random forests.

  Spatially cross-validated predictions explained 58% of the variance
  (RMSE = 6.1 Mg C ha^-1^). Bare-soil composites and the late-summer NDVI
  minimum were the most informative predictors. We discuss implications
  for monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) under the EU Carbon
  Removal Certification Framework.
keywords: [soil organic carbon, remote sensing, "random forest", Sentinel-2, digital soil mapping]
date: 2024-03-15
format:
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
    classoption: [11pt, a4paper]
    keep-tex: true
    number-sections: true
    geometry: [margin=1in]
    linestretch: 1.5
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        \usepackage{lineno}
        \linenumbers
        \usepackage{siunitx}
  docx:
    reference-doc: template.docx
    number-sections: true
bibliography: [refs.bib, software.bib]
csl: https://www.zotero.org/styles/elsevier-harvard
crossref:

  tbl-prefix: Table

---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(ranger)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

samples <- read_csv("data/soc_samples_2019_2022.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cv      <- readRDS("output/spatial_cv_results.rds")
r2      <- cv$r2
rmse    <- cv$rmse
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Soils hold more organic carbon than the atmosphere and terrestrial
vegetation combined [@lal2004; @jobbagy2000], and even small relative
changes in soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks therefore matter for the
global carbon budget. In Mediterranean croplands, where SOC contents are
typically low (often < 1%) and decline under intensive tillage, there is
considerable interest in practices that rebuild SOC, e.g. cover cropping,
reduced tillage and the incorporation of pruning residues
[@aguilera2013; @vicente2020].

Verifying such gains requires baseline maps at the field scale, i.e. at
resolutions of tens of metres rather than the 250 m of global products
such as SoilGrids [@poggio2021]. Digital soil mapping (DSM), which links
point observations to spatially exhaustive covariates, has become the
standard tool for this task [@mcbratney2003]. Among the covariates,
multispectral imagery of bare soil has proven particularly useful, since soil colour and SOC are closely related in the
visible and near-infrared; as @smith2019 [p. 12] put it, "the darker the
soil, the more we expect to find". Sentinel-2, with its five-day revisit
and 10–20 m bands, now makes multi-temporal bare-soil composites feasible
over large areas [@dematte2020; @castaldi2019].

This study had three objectives:

1. to map topsoil (0–30 cm) SOC stocks across a 2,400 km² agricultural
   region of the Guadalquivir valley at 20 m resolution;
2. to quantify the contribution of Sentinel-2 bare-soil and
   vegetation-index composites relative to terrain and legacy soil data;
3. to assess prediction uncertainty with spatial cross-validation and
   quantile regression forests [@meinshausen2006].

# Materials and methods {#sec-methods}

## Study area

The study area (approx. 2,400 km²; @fig-map) lies in the Campiña of the
Córdoba and Sevilla provinces, southern Spain. The climate is
Mediterranean (Köppen Csa) with a mean annual temperature of 17.8 °C and
mean annual precipitation of 540 mm, concentrated between October and
April. Soils are predominantly Vertisols and Calcisols developed on
Miocene marls, with Fluvisols along the river terraces (@tbl-site-chars).
Land use is dominated by rainfed winter cereals and sunflower in rotation,
olive groves and, to a lesser extent, irrigated maize and cotton.

| Land use        | Sites | Mean slope (%) | Clay (%) | Tillage           |
|:----------------|------:|---------------:|---------:|:------------------|
| Rainfed cereals |   168 |            4.2 |       41 | conventional      |
| Olive groves | 121 | 7.9 | 36 | none / cover crop |
| Irrigated maize | 54 | 1.1 | 33 | conventional |
| Sunflower | 69 | 3.8 | 44 | reduced |

: Site characteristics. {#tbl-site-chars}

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Study area and sampling locations (n = 412). Background: Sentinel-2 bare-soil composite (RGB = B4, B3, B2), 2019–2022."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
plot_study_area(samples)  # defined in R/plots.R
```

## Soil sampling and laboratory analyses

Between October 2019 and November 2022, 412 sites were sampled following
a conditioned Latin hypercube design [@minasny2006] stratified by land
use. At each site five cores (0–30 cm) were taken within a 10 m radius
and bulked. SOC was determined by wet oxidation [@walkley1934], and bulk
density (BD) with the core method on a subset of 160 sites; for the
remaining sites BD was predicted with a pedotransfer function fitted to
the measured subset (R² = 0.61)[^ptf]. SOC stocks were then computed as

$$
\mathrm{SOC_{stock}} = \mathrm{SOC} \times \mathrm{BD} \times d \times (1 - \mathrm{CF}) \times 10^{-1}
$$ {#eq-stock}

where SOC is in g kg⁻¹, BD in g cm⁻³, $d$ is the layer thickness (cm),
CF is the volumetric coarse-fragment fraction, and the factor $10^{-1}$
converts the result to Mg C ha⁻¹. Stocks by land use are summarised in
@tbl-sites.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of sampled sites by land use (mean ± s.d.)."
samples |>
  group_by(land_use) |>
  summarise(n     = n(),
            SOC   = sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", mean(soc_gkg), sd(soc_gkg)),
            BD    = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", mean(bd), sd(bd)),
            Stock = sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", mean(stock), sd(stock))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Land use", "n", "SOC (g kg⁻¹)", "BD (g cm⁻³)", "Stock (Mg ha⁻¹)"))
```

## Covariates

We assembled 38 candidate covariates in four groups (@tbl-covariates).
Sentinel-2 Level-2A scenes were cloud-masked with the scene
classification layer and s2cloudless, and a bare-soil composite was
computed as the per-pixel median of all observations with NDVI < 0.25
and NBR2 < 0.075, following @dematte2020. In addition, we computed
seasonal NDVI percentiles (10th, 50th, 90th) to capture crop-type and management differences.

+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Group                 | Source             | Resolution     | Layers |
+=======================+====================+================+========+
| Bare-soil reflectance | Sentinel-2 L2A     | 10–20 m        | 10     |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Vegetation indices    | Sentinel-2 L2A     | 10 m           | 12     |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Terrain               | Copernicus DEM     | 30 m           | 9      |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+
| Legacy soil maps      | REDIAM; SoilGrids  | 1:400k; 250 m  | 7      |
+-----------------------+--------------------+----------------+--------+

: Covariate groups used for model fitting. {#tbl-covariates}

## Model fitting and validation

Random forests were fitted with **ranger** [@wright2017] using 1,000
trees; `mtry` and the minimum node size were tuned by grid search. To
avoid the optimistic bias of random *k*-fold cross-validation under
spatial autocorrelation, we used spatial blocking with 5 km blocks
[@roberts2017] and report the coefficient of determination ($R^2$), the
root mean squared error (RMSE) and Lin's concordance correlation
coefficient (CCC). Prediction intervals were derived from quantile
regression forests, i.e. from the 5th and 95th conditional percentiles.

# Results {#sec-results}

The spatially cross-validated model explained `{r} round(r2, 2)` of the
variance in SOC stocks, with an RMSE of `{r} round(rmse, 1)` Mg C ha⁻¹.
Performance was markedly lower under olive groves than under annual crops
-- a pattern also reported by @castaldi2019 [Fig. 4] for southern Italy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance of the 15 most important covariates. Error bars show the range across the 5 spatial folds."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_importance(cv$importance, top_n = 15)
```

As shown in @fig-importance, the bare-soil SWIR bands (B11, B12) and the
late-summer NDVI minimum dominated, followed by elevation and the
topographic wetness index. Legacy soil maps contributed little once the
Sentinel-2 composites were included.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Our accuracies are comparable to those of other regional studies using
bare-soil composites, e.g. $R^2$ = 0.52–0.64 in @dematte2020 and 0.49 in @castaldi2019, though direct comparisons are hampered by differences in sampling depth, validation design and SOC range. Three caveats apply.

- First, the bare-soil composite is, by construction, biased towards
  fields that are ploughed in late summer.
    - Olive groves with permanent cover are under-represented, which likely explains the weaker performance there.
- Second, BD was measured on only 39% of sites; errors in the
  pedotransfer function propagate directly into stock estimates (@eq-stock).
- Third, the sampling period (2019–2022) includes two drought years, cf.
  the 2022 summer, when NDVI minima were unusually low.

> The question for MRV schemes is not whether remote sensing can replace
> soil sampling, but how few samples it lets us get away with.
>
> > We think the honest answer, for now, is "fewer, but not few".

## Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

We thank the farmers of the Campiña cooperatives for access to their
fields, and Dr. R. Ortega for help with the BD measurements. This work
was funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science (grant PID2020-11xxxx) and
the BMBF project *SOC-Monitor*.

## Data availability {.unnumbered}

Code and derived data are available at <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.0000000>; raw sample
coordinates are withheld at the request of landowners.

# References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

# Appendix {.appendix}

## Hyperparameter grid

```{r}
#| label: tbl-grid
#| tbl-cap: "Tuning grid and selected values (bold)."
kable(cv$tuning_grid)
```

[^ptf]: The pedotransfer function was a linear model of BD on clay, SOC
    and land use. Using the published function of @alexander1980 instead
    changed mean stocks by less than 3%.
