arguments.content:
openapi: "3.0.3"
info:
  title: Regional Food Price Monitor API
  version: '1.2.0'
  # fmt: markdown
  description: |
    Weekly retail prices of staple foods collected by enumerators in **312 markets** across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, maintained by the Development Economics group.  Prices are reported in local currency per standard unit and, where possible, converted to USD at the weekly average exchange rate.

    ## Data use
    * Free for __non-commercial research__; please cite the data paper (see `externalDocs`).
    * Do not redistribute the raw enumerator-level records.
    - Rate limit: 60 requests per minute per API key.

    ## Known issues
    1. Prices for _Rwanda_ before 2016 are monthly, not weekly.
    2. Some markets were renamed after the 2019 boundary revision; join on `marketId`, never on the name.

    | field | unit |
    |---|---|
    | price | local currency per `unit` |
    | price_usd | USD per kg|
  contact:
    name: "Development Economics Group – data team"
    email: foodprices@econ.example.ac.uk
    url: https://foodprices.econ.example.ac.uk
  license:
    name: CC BY-NC 4.0
    url: "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/"
externalDocs:
  description: Data paper (Okello, Brandt & Mwita 2022, Scientific Data)
  url: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-00000-0
servers:
  - url: https://api.foodprices.econ.example.ac.uk/v1
    description: production
  - url: 'http://localhost:8000/v1'
    description: "local dev (uvicorn)"
tags:
  - {name: markets, description: Market locations and metadata}
  - name: prices
    description: Weekly retail price observations
  - name: indices
    description: >
      Derived indices such as the cost of a standard food basket. These are recomputed every Monday,
      so values for the most recent 4 weeks may still change.
security:
  - ApiKeyAuth: []

paths:
  /markets:
    get:
      tags: [markets]
      summary: List markets
      operationId: listMarkets
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/Country'
        - name: admin1
          in: query
          description: First-level administrative unit (county / region / province), spelled as in the 2019 GADM release.
          schema: {type: string}
        - $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit"
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A page of markets
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items: {$ref: '#/components/schemas/Market'}
        "401": {$ref: "#/components/responses/Unauthorized"}

  /markets/{marketId}:
    get:
      tags: [markets]
      summary: Get one market
      operationId: getMarket
      parameters:
        - name: marketId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
            pattern: '^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}$'
          example: KE-0042
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The market
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Market'
        "404":
          description: no market with that id

  /prices:
    get:
      tags:
        - prices
      summary: Query weekly price observations
      description: |
        Returns one row per market × commodity × week. Missing weeks are **not** imputed; use the `/indices` endpoints if you need a complete series.

        Dates are ISO weeks, given as the Monday of the week.
      operationId: queryPrices
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/Country'
        - name: commodity
          in: query
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
            enum: [maize_grain, maize_flour, beans_dry, rice_imported, sorghum, cassava_fresh, matooke, milk_fresh, cooking_oil, sugar]
        - name: from
          in: query
          schema: {type: string, format: date}
          example: "2021-01-04"
        - name: to
          in: query
          schema: {type: string, format: date}
        - name: currency
          in: query
          schema:
            type: string
            enum: ["local", "USD"]
            default: local
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/Limit'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/PriceObservation'
            text/csv:
              schema: {type: string}
        '400':
          description: Bad request, e.g. `from` after `to`, or a date range longer than 10 years
        "401":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/Unauthorized"

components:
  securitySchemes:
    ApiKeyAuth:
      type: apiKey
      in: header
      name: X-API-Key
  parameters:
    Country:
      name: country
      in: query
      description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code
      schema:
        type: string
        enum: [KE, UG, TZ, RW]
    Limit:
      name: limit
      in: query
      schema: {type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 5000, default: 500}
  responses:
    Unauthorized:
      description: "Missing or invalid API key"
  schemas:
    Market:
      type: object
      required: [marketId, name, country]
      properties:
        marketId: {type: string, example: KE-0042}
        name: {type: string, example: "Kisumu Kibuye"}
        country: {type: string, example: KE}
        admin1: {type: string, nullable: true}
        lat: {type: number, format: double, example: -0.0917}
        lon: {type: number, format: double, example: 34.768}
        urban: {type: boolean, example: true}
        first_obs: {type: string, format: date, example: 2008-01-07}
    PriceObservation:
      type: object
      properties:
        marketId:
          type: string
        commodity:
          type: string
        week:
          type: string
          format: date
          description: Monday of the ISO week
        price:
          type: number
          description: Price in local currency per `unit`
        unit:
          type: string
          example: kg
        price_usd:
          type: number
          nullable: true
          description: >-
            Price converted to USD per kg using the weekly mean of the central bank's
            reference rate. Null when the exchange rate is not available for that week.
        n_quotes: {type: integer, description: "number of enumerator price quotes averaged", minimum: 1}
        flags:
          type: array
          items:
            type: string
            enum:
              - imputed_unit_conversion
              - outlier_checked
              - enumerator_comment

date: 2026-10-15
date-modified: last-modified
abstract: "This review compares our contracted parcel carriers on on-time delivery, first-attempt success, damage claims and fully loaded cost per parcel for July to September 2026, and recommends volume shifts for the Q1 2027 allocation round."
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    code-fold: true
    code-tools: {source: false, toggle: true}
    theme: [cosmo, assets/acme.scss]
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height:   4.5
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrreprt
    papersize: a4
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  freeze: auto
bibliography: references.bib
csl: "https://www.zotero.org/styles/apa"
crossref: {fig-prefix: Figure, tbl-prefix: Table, sec-prefix: Section}
params:
  quarter: "2026-Q3"
  carriers: [DHL, DPD, GLS, UPS, "Hermes"]
  min_parcels: 5000
---

## Executive summary {#sec-summary}

On-time delivery across the network recovered to **94.1%** in Q3 (Q2: 91.7%), driven almost entirely by DPD and GLS after the Hamburg cross-dock reopened in mid-July.  UPS remains the most reliable carrier for next-day B2B lanes but is also the most expensive per parcel, and Hermes continues to lag on first-attempt delivery in rural postcode areas [@acme_network_2026; @mckinnon2015green, ch. 4].

::: {.callout-important}
## Recommendation
Shift roughly 8% of B2C volume in the *South* region from Hermes to GLS in the Q1 2027 allocation round, subject to the GLS capacity confirmation due on 2026-11-28.  Keep UPS for next-day B2B lanes despite the cost premium (see @sec-cost).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How to read this report
All figures are computed from scan events in the tracking platform (topic `shipment.events.v2`), not from carrier invoices.   Cost per parcel uses the _fully loaded_ rate: base tariff plus fuel surcharge[^fuel], residential surcharge and any re-delivery fees.
:::

## Data and method {#sec-method}

We use all parcels handed over between 2026-07-01 and 2026-09-30, excluding returns and parcels without a first carrier scan (about 0.4% of volume).  A parcel is *on time* if the first successful delivery scan happens on or before the promised date shown to the customer at checkout.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
shipments <- arrow::read_parquet("data/shipments_2026q3.parquet") |>
  filter(n_parcels >= params$min_parcels)
```

The analysis covers `r format(nrow(shipments), big.mark = ",")` parcels from `r n_distinct(shipments$depot_id)` depots and `r n_distinct(shipments$lane_id)` lanes.

Lane
:   An origin depot and a destination postcode area (first two digits), e.g. `HAM-80`.

First-attempt success (FAS)
:    Share of parcels delivered at the first attempt, i.e. without a "not at home" or "no access" scan.

On-time rate (OTR)
: Parcels delivered on or before the promised date, divided by all delivered parcels.

For carrier $c$ in week $w$, the on-time rate is

$$
\text{OTR}_{c,w} = \frac{1}{|P_{c,w}|} \sum_{i \in P_{c,w}} \mathbb{1}\left[d_i \le p_i\right]
$$

where $d_i$ is the delivery date and $p_i$ the promised date of parcel $i$.

## Results

### On-time delivery ###

```{r}
#| label: fig-ontime
#| fig-cap: "Weekly on-time rate by carrier, Q3 2026. The shaded band marks the Hamburg cross-dock closure (weeks 27 to 29)."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with one line per carrier showing weekly on-time rates between 85 and 98 percent. DPD and GLS rise sharply after week 29, while Hermes stays below 90 percent for the whole quarter."
#| fig-width:   9
shipments |>
  weekly_otr(by = carrier) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, otr, colour = carrier)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 27, xmax = 29, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

@fig-ontime shows the recovery after week 29 very clearly. The dip for UPS in week 33 is an artefact: a scanner firmware update in the Munich hub delayed delivery scans by up to six hours, which pushed some same-day deliveries past midnight.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### By region

| Region | Parcels | On-time | FAS | Damage claims per 10k |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|---:|
| North | 1,204,331 | 95.2% | 91.0% | 3.1 |
| South |  987,410 | 92.8% | 86.4% | 4.0 |
| East | 641,002|93.9%|89.7%|2.7 |
| West | 1,410,876 | 94.6% | 90.2% | 3.5 |

: On-time rate and first-attempt success by region {#tbl-region}

#### By carrier

```{r}
#| label: tbl-carriers
#| tbl-cap: Carrier scorecard, Q3 2026
#| tbl-colwidths: [20,16,16,16,16,16]
carrier_scorecard(shipments) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(otr, fas), decimals = 1)
```

:::

### Damage claims

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Damage claims per 10,000 parcels by carrier and weight class](figures/damage-claims.png){#fig-damage fig-alt="Grouped bar chart of damage claims per ten thousand parcels for five carriers across three weight classes. Heavy Hermes parcels have the highest rate at about seven claims per ten thousand." width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Damage claims are rare but expensive: the average settled claim in Q3 was EUR 84.20, and the long tail is driven by bulky items such as furniture and e-bikes (see @fig-damage).  Claims for parcels over 20 kg are three times as likely with Hermes as with DPD.
:::
::::

### Cost per parcel {#sec-cost}

```{r cost-per-parcel, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Fully loaded cost per parcel by carrier and service level, Q3 2026"}
cost_plot(shipments, by = c("carrier", "service_level"))
```

```{python}
#| label: lane-sensitivity
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show the lane sensitivity calculation"
import pandas as pd

lanes = pd.read_parquet("data/lanes_2026q3.parquet")
lanes["shift_saving_eur"] = (lanes.cost_hermes - lanes.cost_gls) * lanes.parcels * 0.08
print(lanes.nlargest(10, "shift_saving_eur")[["lane_id", "parcels", "shift_saving_eur"]])
```

Shifting 8% of South-region B2C volume from Hermes to GLS saves an estimated EUR 212,000 per quarter at current tariffs, assuming GLS keeps its Q3 on-time rate. The simulation used these allocation parameters:

```yaml
allocation_round: 2027-Q1
region:   South
shifts:
  - {from: Hermes, to: GLS, share: 0.08, segment: B2C}
constraints: {gls_max_daily_parcels: 41000, keep_ups_for: [next_day_b2b], max_shift_per_lane: 0.15}
```

## Limitations

- Promised dates shown at checkout are themselves estimates; a carrier with conservative promises looks better on OTR than one with aggressive promises. We do not correct for this, although McKinnon recommends doing so [-@mckinnon2015green].
- Scan data from Hermes arrives in batches, so roughly 2% of its delivery scans are timestamped up to three hours late (@lee2024scanlag found similar lags for other carriers).
-   Damage claims are counted when they are filed, not when the parcel was shipped.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Appendix {.appendix}

{{< include _carrier_contracts.qmd >}}

[^fuel]: Fuel surcharges are indexed monthly to the diesel price published by the Federal Statistical Office.  For Q3 they ranged from 14.5% (DHL) to 19.25% (Hermes) of the base tariff.

---
title: "Authorization latency regression: post-incident analysis"
subtitle: 'INC-2026-1103 (Sev-2)'
author: ["Dr. Amara Okafor", "J. P. Lindqvist"]
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: {collapsed: false}
    df_print: kable
    code_folding:    hide
params:
  incident_id: INC-2026-1103
  window_start: "2026-11-03 13:40:00"
  window_end:   "2026-11-03 16:05:00"
  baseline_days: 14
bibliography: refs.bib
link-citations: yes
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
    canonical: true
  chunk_output_type: console
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
source("R/latency_helpers.R")
auth <- read_auth_events(params$window_start, params$window_end, baseline_days = params$baseline_days)
```

# Summary

On 3 November 2026 between 13:40 and 16:05 CET, the 99th percentile of card authorization latency at the payments gateway rose from approx. 420 ms to more than 2.3 s. The regression affected all card schemes, but it was most visible for Mastercard transactions routed via the U.K. acquirer (see Fig. 2). Approximately 18,400 authorizations (about 1.7% of attempts in the window) timed out, and an estimated EUR 1.1m of checkout value was lost or delayed. No card data was exposed, and no duplicate captures were found during reconciliation the next morning.

Dr. Okafor's team first suspected the new 3-D Secure challenge flow, i.e. the change that shipped in release v4.18.0 that morning; however, the timing did not match. The root cause turned out to be connection-pool exhaustion in the HSM proxy, a component whose pooling code had not been touched since 2009. It was triggered by a routine certificate rotation on the HSM cluster, which made every TLS handshake about four times slower (see Sec. 3.2 for details).

## Timeline

All times are CET. The timeline was reconstructed from PagerDuty, the `#inc-2026-1103` Slack channel and the gateway's audit log; where those sources disagree, the audit log wins.

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 13:40 | p99 latency crosses the 800 ms SLO threshold. |
| 13:52 | First page to the payments on-call (Mr. Lindqvist). |
| 14:20 | Incident declared Sev-2; comms lead assigned. |
| 15:31 | HSM proxy pool size raised from 64 to 256 via config flag. |
| 16:05 | p99 back below 450 ms; monitoring continues. |

## Impact

```{r latency-plot, fig.cap="p99 authorization latency by acquirer on 3 November 2026. The shaded band is the incident window. Note the log scale.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
plot_latency(auth, by = "acquirer", log_y = TRUE, highlight = c(params$window_start, params$window_end))
```

The effect differed considerably by acquirer and scheme (Fig. 1 vs. Fig. 2). Visa transactions through the EU acquirer saw a moderate increase, e.g. from 380 ms to roughly 900 ms at p99, whereas Mastercard through the U.K. acquirer exceeded the 2 s client timeout for long stretches. In total, `r format(sum(auth$timed_out), big.mark = ",")` authorizations timed out. The merchants most affected were large ticketing customers running flash sales, which have little tolerance for retries...

```{r}
#| label: tbl-impact
#| tbl-cap: "Impact by card scheme. Counts are approx. and exclude client-side retries."
impact_table(auth) |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

Some customers retried aggressively. This is _expected_ behaviour, and our client libraries back off exponentially (cf. the retry policy in Sec. 4 of the integration guide). However, at least one large merchant (No. 7 in the internal ranking) uses a custom integration that retries immediately, which roughly tripled its request volume during the incident. Did the retries make things worse? Probably, but only marginally: they added about 6% to the load on the HSM proxy.

## Root cause

The HSM proxy keeps a fixed-size pool of TLS connections to the hardware security modules. When the HSM cluster's certificate was rotated at 13:35, all pooled connections were closed and re-established at once. With the new 4096-bit key, each handshake took approx. 180 ms instead of 45 ms. Because the pool size (64) had been tuned years ago for a much lower request rate, requests queued behind the handshakes and the latency cascaded through the gateway.

> "We had a runbook for HSM certificate rotation, but it assumed the proxy would reconnect lazily. It does not. It reconnects everything at once." -- Mr. Lindqvist, in the incident channel at 15:12

Several factors contributed:

1. The rotation was scheduled during business hours (14:00 is our lowest-traffic hour on weekdays, but only for EU merchants).
2. The proxy's pool metrics were not on any dashboard. They were only exposed via JMX, i.e. invisible to Grafana.
3. The canary for the rotation checked HSM health, not end-to-end authorization latency. It passed.

This is a well-known failure pattern for connection pools under synchronized reconnects [@nygard2018release, pp. 112-118; @kleppmann2017designing]. Similar incidents have been described at other payment providers, e.g. in a 2019 talk by Dr. Chen et al. on "thundering herds" in HSM fleets [-@chen2019herds].

## Action items

* **Pool sizing.** Make the pool size adaptive, with a floor of 128. Owner: payments-core. Due 2026-12-15.
* **Staggered reconnects.** Reconnect at most 10% of the pool per second after a rotation. This should have been the default all along.
* **Dashboards.** Export the pool metrics to Prometheus and add them to the _Gateway Golden Signals_ dashboard.
* __Rotation runbook.__ Move HSM certificate rotations to the 03:00-05:00 window, and add an end-to-end latency check to the canary.

The estimated cost of the action items is approx. 3 engineer-weeks. Given that a similar rotation is scheduled for Q1 2027, we recommend completing at least the first two items before then. Questions should go to Dr. Okafor or to the #payments-core channel.

## Appendix: method

Latency percentiles were computed per minute from the gateway's request logs (n = `r nrow(auth)` requests in the window, plus a 14-day baseline). We used the t-digest implementation in the **tdigest** package [@dunning2019tdigest] with compression 200, which keeps the relative error at p99 below 0.5% for our volumes. The baseline is the median of the same minute-of-day across the previous 14 days, excl. public holidays (e.g. 1 Nov.).[^holidays]

[^holidays]: All Saints' Day (1 Nov.) is a public holiday in several German states. Traffic on that day is not representative. We therefore excluded it from the baseline.

```{r appendix-session, echo=TRUE, results="markup", comment=""}
sessionInfo()
```

The root cause turned out to be connection-pool exhaustion in the HSM proxy, a component whose pooling code had not been touched since 2009. It was triggered by a routine certificate rotation on the HSM cluster, which made every TLS handshake about four times slower (see Sec. 3.2 for details).

## Timeline

All times are CET. The timeline was reconstructed from PagerDuty, the `#inc-2026-1103` Slack channel and the gateway's audit log; where those sources disagree, the audit log wins.

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 13:40 | p99 latency crosses the 800 ms SLO threshold. |
| 13:52 | First page to the payments on-call (Mr. Lindqvist). |
| 14:20 | Incident declared Sev-2; comms lead assigned. |
| 15:31 | HSM proxy pool size raised from 64 to 256 via config flag. |
| 16:05 | p99 back below 450 ms; monitoring continues. |

## Impact

```{r latency-plot, fig.cap="p99 authorization latency by acquirer on 3 November 2026. The shaded band is the incident window. Note the log scale.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
plot_latency(auth, by = "acquirer", log_y = TRUE, highlight = c(params$window_start, params$window_end))
```

The effect differed considerably by acquirer and scheme (Fig. 1 vs. Fig. 2). Visa transactions through the EU acquirer saw a moderate increase, e.g. from 380 ms to roughly 900 ms at p99, whereas Mastercard through the U.K. acquirer exceeded the 2 s client timeout for long stretches. In total, `r format(sum(auth$timed_out), big.mark = ",")` authorizations timed out. The merchants most affected were large ticketing customers running flash sales, which have little tolerance for retries...

```{r}
#| label: tbl-impact
#| tbl-cap: "Impact by card scheme. Counts are approx. and exclude client-side retries."
impact_table(auth) |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

Some customers retried aggressively. This is _expected_ behaviour, and our client libraries back off exponentially (cf. the retry policy in Sec. 4 of the integration guide). However, at least one large merchant (No. 7 in the internal ranking) uses a custom integration that retries immediately, which roughly tripled its request volume during the incident. Did the retries make things worse? Probably, but only marginally: they added about 6% to the load on the HSM proxy.

## Root cause

The HSM proxy keeps a fixed-size pool of TLS connections to the hardware security modules. When the HSM cluster's certificate was rotated at 13:35, all pooled connections were closed and re-established at once. With the new 4096-bit key, each handshake took approx. 180 ms instead of 45 ms. Because the pool size (64) had been tuned years ago for a much lower request rate, requests queued behind the handshakes and the latency cascaded through the gateway.

> "We had a runbook for HSM certificate rotation, but it assumed the proxy would reconnect lazily. It does not. It reconnects everything at once." -- Mr. Lindqvist, in the incident channel at 15:12

Several factors contributed:

1. The rotation was scheduled during business hours (14:00 is our lowest-traffic hour on weekdays, but only for EU merchants).
2. The proxy's pool metrics were not on any dashboard. They were only exposed via JMX, i.e. invisible to Grafana.
3. The canary for the rotation checked HSM health, not end-to-end authorization latency. It passed.

This is a well-known failure pattern for connection pools under synchronized reconnects [@nygard2018release, pp. 112-118; @kleppmann2017designing]. Similar incidents have been described at other payment providers, e.g. in a 2019 talk by Dr. Chen et al. on "thundering herds" in HSM fleets [-@chen2019herds].

## Action items

* **Pool sizing.** Make the pool size adaptive, with a floor of 128. Owner: payments-core. Due 2026-12-15.
* **Staggered reconnects.** Reconnect at most 10% of the pool per second after a rotation. This should have been the default all along.
* **Dashboards.** Export the pool metrics to Prometheus and add them to the _Gateway Golden Signals_ dashboard.
* __Rotation runbook.__ Move HSM certificate rotations to the 03:00-05:00 window, and add an end-to-end latency check to the canary.

The estimated cost of the action items is approx. 3 engineer-weeks. Given that a similar rotation is scheduled for Q1 2027, we recommend completing at least the first two items before then. Questions should go to Dr. Okafor or to the #payments-core channel.

## Appendix: method

Latency percentiles were computed per minute from the gateway's request logs (n = `r nrow(auth)` requests in the window, plus a 14-day baseline). We used the t-digest implementation in the **tdigest** package [@dunning2019tdigest] with compression 200, which keeps the relative error at p99 below 0.5% for our volumes. The baseline is the median of the same minute-of-day across the previous 14 days, excl. public holidays (e.g. 1 Nov.).[^holidays]

[^holidays]: All Saints' Day (1 Nov.) is a public holiday in several German states. Traffic on that day is not representative. We therefore excluded it from the baseline.

```{r appendix-session, echo=TRUE, results="markup", comment=""}
sessionInfo()
```

arguments.content:
Changelog
=========

All notable changes to **Tidy Chests** are documented here. The format is (loosely) based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ "Keep a Changelog 1.1.0"), and the mod uses [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/), which for a Stardew mod mostly means "the major version goes up when I break your config".
If you're updating from 1.x, read the 2.0.0 notes first, *please*, it'll save us both a Nexus comment.  

## [Unreleased]

### Added
- Controller support for the sort button (finally!) — it's on <kbd>Right Stick</kbd> press by default and can be changed in GMCM
- Italian translation, thanks to _Giulia_ :it:
+ `sortJunimoChests` option, off by default because Junimo chests are shared between all of them and sorting them in multiplayer surprised a lot of people who were not expecting their stuff to move around while they were standing right there

### Fixed
* The fridge in the farmhouse no longer gets sorted into the mini-fridge (#87)
* Sorting a chest with exactly 36 items no longer drops the last item on the floor. Nobody lost anything valuable as far as I know, but if you did, sorry!!

## [2.1.0] - 2024-03-30 ##

### Added

- New sort mode **"by category, then quality"**, which is what most people asked for in the poll:
  1. category (crops, artisan goods, fish, ...)
  2. quality, iridium first
  3. name
- The GMCM page has a live preview now   

![the new sort button](docs/images/sort-button.png "The sort button, top right next to the colour picker")

### Changed

- The default hotkey moved from `S` to `Shift+S`, because `S` is also "move down" for about half of you. Yes, I should have thought about that in 1.0.
- ~~Chests are sorted when you open them~~ Chests are sorted when you __close__ them, so you can actually see what you're doing.

| Action | Old default | New default |
|---|:---:|---|
| Sort | `S` | `Shift+S` |
| Toggle auto-sort|none| `Shift+A` |
| Undo last sort | `Ctrl+Z` |`Ctrl+Z` (unchanged)|

### Removed

- The `legacySort` option. It's been deprecated since 1.6 and the code was getting in the way of everything else.

***

2.0.0 — 2024-01-14
------------------

:warning: **Breaking:** the config format changed. The mod migrates your old `config.json` automatically on first launch and keeps a backup as `config.json.bak`, but if you edited it by hand you might want to double check the result. Old vs. new:

~~~json
{ "SortKey": "S", "SortOnOpen": true, "IgnoredChests": ["Fridge"] }
~~~

```json
{
  "Hotkeys": { "Sort": "LeftShift + S" },
  "SortWhen": "Close",
  "Ignore": { "ChestNames": ["Fridge"], "Junimo": true }
}
```

When the migration runs you'll see this in the SMAPI console:

    [Tidy Chests] Migrated config.json (v1 -> v2), backup saved as config.json.bak
    [Tidy Chests] 3 ignored chest names carried over

#### Added
* Per-chest ignore: put `#nosort` anywhere in a chest's name, e.g. `Seeds #nosort`. Chest names ending in \* are treated the same way, for people who were already doing that with the old *Chest Labels* mod
* Compatibility with *Chests Anywhere* and *Automate*[^automate]

#### Fixed
* crash when sorting while a festival is loading (only on Android?)
* coloured chests losing their colour after sorting :bug:

Known issues that are still open, numbered the same as in the pinned Nexus post:

4. Sorting Ginger Island chests sometimes needs a second click
5. The GMCM preview is wrong for stacks over 999
7. Big chests (1.6) sort fine but the preview only shows the first 36 slots

## 1.6.2 - 2023-09-02
- fix: compatibility with SMAPI 3.18.5  
- fix: typo in the German translation ("Kiste", not "Kist")

## 1.6.0 - 2023-07-21
- sort button in the chest menu
- `legacySort` is deprecated and will be removed in 2.x
- the mod now needs SMAPI 3.18 or later\
  (older versions log an error and skip loading the mod)

- - -

Older versions (1.0 – 1.5) were before I kept a changelog. The short version: it sorted chests. Sometimes correctly. If you really want to know, the commit history on [GitHub][repo] goes all the way back, typos and all. :tada:

<!-- fmt: off -->
Compatibility matrix -- keep this aligned by hand please:

| Tidy Chests | Stardew | SMAPI  |
|-------------|---------|--------|
| 2.1.x       | 1.6.x   | 4.0+   |
| 2.0.x       | 1.6.x   | 4.0+   |
| 1.6.x       | 1.5.6   | 3.18+  |
<!-- fmt: on -->

___

[^automate]: Automate moves items around on its own schedule, so if an Automate machine is connected to a chest, Tidy Chests skips that chest instead of fighting it. You can turn that off with `"RespectAutomate": false` in the config, but I really wouldn't.

[2.1.0]: https://github.com/mossfeather/TidyChests/compare/v2.0.0...v2.1.0
[repo]: https://github.com/mossfeather/TidyChests  "Tidy Chests on GitHub"

--- title: "Contributing" weight: 90 draft: false aliases: [ /docs/contributing/, "/hacking/" ] description: "How to build teacup from source, run the tests, and get a pull request merged without too much back-and-forth. Please skim this before opening a big PR, it'll save us both time." --- # Contributing to teacup # First off: thanks for even opening this file! :tea: teacup is a one-person hobby project (hi, I'm Rosa) that somehow turned into a thing a few hundred people use for their blogs, and every bug report, typo fix, theme and PR genuinely helps. That said, I work on this in the evenings and at weekends, so please be patient if I don't reply for a week or two; it's not personal, I promise. Small PRs get merged faster than big ones. If you want to do something big, open an issue first so we can talk about it *before* you sink a weekend into it. Getting set up ============== You need: + Go 1.22 or newer + `make` (on Windows use WSL, or just run the commands from the `Makefile` by hand) + optionally [`watchexec`](https://github.com/watchexec/watchexec "watchexec on GitHub") for `make watch` Then: 1) fork the repo and clone your fork 2) `make build` — this produces `./bin/teacup` 3) `make test` — runs the unit tests *and* the golden-file tests in `testdata/sites/` 4) `./bin/teacup serve ./examples/blog` and open http://localhost:1313 If step 3 fails on a fresh clone, that's a bug. Please tell me! ## Project layout ```text cmd/teacup/ CLI entry point (cobra) internal/build/ the actual site builder internal/markdown/ goldmark setup + our extensions (callouts, footnotes, heading ids) internal/theme/ template loading; the default theme is in internal/theme/default/ testdata/sites/ golden-file tests, each folder is a tiny site + its expected output ``` ### Golden-file tests Each folder under `testdata/sites/` has a `site/` and an `expected/` directory. The test builds `site/` and diffs the output against `expected/`. When you change the output on purpose, regenerate the expected files with: UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/build/... and then **look at the diff** before committing it. I have merged broken golden files before because I didn't look. Don't be me. ### Testing with a real site Most bugs only show up with real content, so it helps to test against a site with a config like this one (it turns on most of the optional features): ```yaml # teacup.yaml title: "Rosa's test blog" baseURL: http://localhost:1313/ theme: default paginate: 10 markdown: smartypants: true footnotes: yes callouts: [note, tip, warning, danger] taxonomies: { tags: tag, series: series } feeds: - {type: atom, path: /feed.xml, limit: 20} - type: json path: /feed.json build: drafts: false future: False minify: ~ ``` ## Commit messages & PRs I don't care much about commit message format, but please make the PR description useful. The template in `.github/pull_request_template.md` looks like this, fill it in and delete whatever doesn't apply: ````markdown ## What does this change? ## ## Checklist * [ ] `make test` passes * [ ] golden files updated (and I actually looked at the diff) * [ ] docs updated if behaviour changed + [ ] added myself to `CONTRIBUTORS.md` if I wanted to ```` ## Code style `gofmt` and `go vet` are enforced in CI, `golangci-lint` runs too but only as a warning for now. Beyond that: - keep functions short-ish; if you need to scroll, split it - errors: wrap them with `fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err)`, don't log *and* return - no new dependencies without asking first. teacup's whole point is being small: - the binary is ~9 MB and I'd like to keep it under 15 - `go.sum` currently has 23 lines, it was 210 before I dropped the second markdown library[^deps] > **A note on themes** > > Themes don't live in this repo anymore (except the default one). Publish yours as a separate repo with the `teacup-theme` topic and it'll show up on the [themes page][themes]. Please don't send PRs that add themes here, I'll politely close them. ### Makefile targets | target | what | notes| |--|--|--| | `make build` | build `./bin/teacup` | uses `-trimpath` | | `make test` | unit + golden tests | | | `make watch` | rebuild and re-serve the example blog on every change | needs watchexec | | `make release` | cross-compile for linux/mac/windows, amd64 + arm64 | **maintainers only**, needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` | ## Reporting bugs Please include the output of `teacup version`, your OS, and ideally a tiny site that reproduces the problem (a zip, or a link to a repo). "My site doesn't build" with no details makes me sad :cry:.
Why does teacup version print a git hash? Release builds embed the commit they were built from. If you see `(devel)` you built from source without `make`, which is fine, but tell me which commit you're on.
## Code of conduct Be kind. That's basically it. The longer version is in [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md); TL;DR: no harassment, no gatekeeping, assume good intent, and remember there's a human on the other end who's doing this for fun. --- _Thanks again for helping out_ — Rosa\ teacup is MIT licensed; by contributing you agree your code is too. [^deps]: Not because the library was bad! It was great. It just pulled in half of the internet for a feature (math rendering) that four people used, and those four people can use KaTeX on the client side. [themes]: https://teacup.example.dev/themes/ "Community themes"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# fmt: markdown
"""Reconcile PSP settlement files against the internal ledger.

This script is run by the **payments-ops** cron (`ops/cron/settlement.yaml`) every morning at 06:15 CET, after all payment service providers have dropped their settlement reports into the `s3://acme-pay-settlement-inbox` bucket.  It can also be run by hand when a PSP re-sends a corrected file.

Usage
-----

    python reconcile_settlements.py --psp adyen --date 2026-11-16 --dry-run

What it does:
* downloads the settlement report for the given PSP and business date,
* normalises every line into a `SettlementLine` (amounts in minor units),
+ matches lines to ledger postings, see *Matching rules* below,
* writes unmatched items to `recon.exceptions` and posts a summary to the payments-ops channel.

Exit codes: `0` if everything matched, `3` if exceptions were found (not an error, but somebody has to look at them), `1` for anything else.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import datetime as dt
import io
import logging
import os
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable, Iterator

import boto3
import psycopg
import requests
import yaml

log = logging.getLogger("recon")

INBOX_BUCKET = os.environ.get("RECON_INBOX_BUCKET", "acme-pay-settlement-inbox")
TEAMS_WEBHOOK = os.environ.get("RECON_TEAMS_WEBHOOK", "")

# Defaults; override with --config path/to/recon.yaml (merged one level deep).
DEFAULT_CONFIG_YAML = """
psp:
  adyen:   {prefix: adyen/settlement, glob: "settlement_detail_report_batch_*.csv", delimiter: ","}
  stripe:
    prefix: stripe/payouts
    glob: 'payout_reconciliation_*.csv'
  worldpay: {prefix: worldpay/eod, glob: "*.EOD", delimiter: "|"}
matching:
  fuzzy_window_days: 1
  batch_psps: [sepa_dd]
notify:
    channel: "#payments-ops"
    mention_on_exceptions: ["@pay-oncall"]
"""

# fmt: markdown
CONFIG_HELP = r"""
## Configuration file

The file passed with `--config` is merged **one level deep** into the defaults, so you only need to list what you want to change.  For example, to widen the fuzzy window for a PSP that is known to settle late and to silence the on-call mention:

```yaml
matching:
    fuzzy_window_days:   3
notify: {mention_on_exceptions: []}
```

Unknown top-level keys are rejected with exit code `1`, so typos do not go unnoticed.
"""

# fmt: markdown
# ## Matching rules
#
# Matching runs in passes, from the most to the least specific.   A line matched in an earlier pass is never reconsidered, which keeps the result deterministic even when a PSP sends duplicate references.
#
# 1. **Exact** -- the PSP reference equals the ledger posting's `external_ref`.
# 2. **Fuzzy** -- same merchant, currency and amount, value date within `fuzzy_window_days` days.
#    Ties go to the earliest ledger posting.
# 3. **Batch** -- for PSPs that settle in aggregate (looking at you, SEPA direct debit), compare per-merchant daily totals instead of individual lines.
#
# Anything left over becomes a row in `recon.exceptions` with reason `UNMATCHED`.


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SettlementLine:
    psp: str
    psp_reference: str
    merchant_id: str
    currency: str
    amount_minor: int
    value_date: dt.date
    fee_minor: int = 0


@dataclass
class ReconResult:
    matched: list[tuple[SettlementLine, str]] = field(default_factory=list)
    unmatched: list[SettlementLine] = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def exit_code(self) -> int:
        return 3 if self.unmatched else 0

    def totals_by_currency(self) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
        totals: dict[str, list[int]] = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
        for line, _ in self.matched:
            totals[line.currency][0] += line.amount_minor
            totals[line.currency][1] += line.fee_minor
        return {cur: (net, fees) for cur, (net, fees) in sorted(totals.items())}


def load_config(path: Path | None) -> dict:
    config = yaml.safe_load(DEFAULT_CONFIG_YAML)
    if path is None:
        return config
    override = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) or {}
    unknown = set(override) - set(config)
    if unknown:
        raise SystemExit(f"unknown config keys: {', '.join(sorted(unknown))}")
    for key, value in override.items():
        config[key] = {**config[key], **value}
    return config


def fetch_report(psp: str, business_date: dt.date, cfg: dict) -> Iterator[dict[str, str]]:
    s3 = boto3.client("s3")
    prefix = f"{cfg['psp'][psp]['prefix']}/{business_date:%Y/%m/%d}/"
    for obj in s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket=INBOX_BUCKET, Prefix=prefix).get("Contents", []):
        body = s3.get_object(Bucket=INBOX_BUCKET, Key=obj["Key"])["Body"].read().decode("utf-8-sig")
        yield from csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(body), delimiter=cfg["psp"][psp].get("delimiter", ","))


def to_minor(value: str | None) -> int:
    return int(Decimal(value or "0").scaleb(2))


def normalise(psp: str, rows: Iterable[dict[str, str]]) -> list[SettlementLine]:
    return [
        SettlementLine(
            psp=psp,
            psp_reference=row["Psp Reference"].strip(),
            merchant_id=row["Merchant Account"],
            currency=row["Net Currency"],
            amount_minor=to_minor(row["Net Credit (NC)"]),
            value_date=dt.date.fromisoformat(row["Booking Date"][:10]),
            fee_minor=to_minor(row.get("Commission (NC)")),
        )
        for row in rows
        if row.get("Type", "Settled") in {"Settled", "SettledBulk"}
    ]


def match(lines: list[SettlementLine], conn: psycopg.Connection, cfg: dict) -> ReconResult:
    # fmt: markdown
    # Passes 1 and 2 only.  The *batch* pass for `sepa_dd` is tracked in PAY-2210; until it lands, SEPA direct debit lines that settle in aggregate show up as exceptions and have to be cleared by payments-ops by hand.
    result = ReconResult()
    window = dt.timedelta(days=cfg["matching"]["fuzzy_window_days"])
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        for line in lines:
            cur.execute(
                "SELECT posting_id FROM ledger.postings WHERE external_ref = %s AND NOT reconciled",
                (line.psp_reference,),
            )
            row = cur.fetchone()
            if row is None:
                cur.execute(
                    """
                    SELECT posting_id FROM ledger.postings
                    WHERE merchant_id = %s AND currency = %s AND amount_minor = %s
                      AND value_date BETWEEN %s AND %s AND NOT reconciled
                    ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1
                    """,
                    (line.merchant_id, line.currency, line.amount_minor, line.value_date - window, line.value_date + window),
                )
                row = cur.fetchone()
            (result.matched.append((line, row[0])) if row else result.unmatched.append(line))
    return result


def render_summary(result: ReconResult, psp: str, business_date: dt.date) -> str:
    rows = "\n".join(
        f"| {cur} | {net / 100:,.2f} | {fees / 100:,.2f} |" for cur, (net, fees) in result.totals_by_currency().items()
    )
    # fmt: markdown
    return f"""
### Settlement reconciliation: {psp} / {business_date:%Y-%m-%d}

Matched **{len(result.matched)}** lines; **{len(result.unmatched)}** need attention.   Amounts are net of PSP fees, so they will not match the gross figures shown in the PSP portal.

| Currency | Net settled | Fees |
|---|--:|--:|
{rows}

_Generated by reconcile_settlements.py at {dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc):%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC._
"""


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    # fmt: markdown
    epilog = """
        Examples:

        * re-run yesterday's Adyen file without writing anything:
          `reconcile_settlements.py --psp adyen --date yesterday --dry-run`
        * reconcile a corrected Worldpay file that arrived late, replacing the exceptions from the first run: `reconcile_settlements.py --psp worldpay --date 2026-11-14 --force`
        """
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0], epilog=epilog, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    parser.add_argument("--psp", required=True, choices=["adyen", "stripe", "worldpay", "sepa_dd"])
    parser.add_argument("--date", default="yesterday", help="business date, YYYY-MM-DD or 'yesterday'")
    parser.add_argument("--config", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--force", action="store_true", help="replace exceptions from an earlier run")
    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
    business_date = dt.date.today() - dt.timedelta(days=1) if args.date == "yesterday" else dt.date.fromisoformat(args.date)
    cfg = load_config(args.config)
    lines = normalise(args.psp, fetch_report(args.psp, business_date, cfg))
    log.info("loaded %d settlement lines for %s on %s", len(lines), args.psp, business_date)
    with psycopg.connect(os.environ["LEDGER_DSN"]) as conn:
        result = match(lines, conn, cfg)
        if not args.dry_run:
            write_exceptions(conn, result.unmatched, replace=args.force)
    summary = render_summary(result, args.psp, business_date)
    if TEAMS_WEBHOOK and not args.dry_run:
        requests.post(TEAMS_WEBHOOK, json={"text": summary}, timeout=10).raise_for_status()
    else:
        print(summary)
    return result.exit_code


# %%
#| label: explore-exceptions
#| echo:   false
#| tags: [debug,  interactive]
#| fig-cap: "Unmatched settlement lines by currency for yesterday's Adyen file (interactive session only)"
if "ipykernel" in sys.modules:
    import pandas as pd

    _lines = normalise("adyen", fetch_report("adyen", dt.date.today() - dt.timedelta(days=1), load_config(None)))
    pd.DataFrame([vars(l) for l in _lines]).groupby("currency").amount_minor.sum().plot.bar()

# %%
if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3

# fmt: markdown
"""
Wastewater surveillance pipeline -- weekly sitrep
=================================================

Normalises SARS-CoV-2 N1 gene copy concentrations from the treatment plants by the faecal indicator **PMMoV**, smooths each normalised series with LOWESS and compares the trend with reported case counts for every sewershed.  Run it every Tuesday after the lab has uploaded the qPCR results to the shared drive.

Run it as a script

    python ww_pipeline.py --week 2024-W11 --plants ALV BRG

or render it with `quarto render ww_pipeline.py`, which executes the `# %%` cells below and gives you an HTML version with the plots.

What it does:

1. read the qPCR export (one CSV per plant)
2. drop samples that failed QC (inhibition control shifted by more than 2 Cq, or amplification in the extraction blank)
3) normalise, log-transform and smooth
4. write `results/<week>/` plus the Markdown summary that goes into the sitrep

* Author: Ines Carvalho (Environmental Epidemiology), with bits of Malik's thesis code
+ Questions: ask Ines, not Malik -- he has graduated :)
"""

#| echo:   false
#| warning: false

import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yaml

log = logging.getLogger("ww_pipeline")
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")

DATA_DIR = Path("/mnt/shared/wastewater/qpcr_exports")
RESULTS_DIR = Path("results")

# fmt: off
# Defaults, overridden by --config.  Keep in sync with config/example.yaml !!
DEFAULT_CONFIG = yaml.safe_load("""
qc:
  max_cq_shift: 2.0      # cycles
  min_pmmov:    1.0e+05  # copies/L
  blank_max_copies: 0
smoothing: {frac: 0.3, it: 1}
plants:   [ALV, BRG, CSN, DLF, ESK]
population: {ALV: 412000, BRG: 96500, CSN: 151200, DLF: 38900, ESK: 72300}
""")
# fmt: on

# fmt: markdown
# ## QC thresholds
#
# These come from the national wastewater SOP (v3.2, section 4.4) and were agreed with the lab in January 2024.  If you change them, **tell the lab** and say so in the methods section of the sitrep, otherwise the trend lines shift and nobody notices until the regional team asks why.
#
# * `max_cq_shift` -- samples whose inhibition control (spiked bovine coronavirus) is shifted by more than this many cycles from the plant median are dropped
# * `min_pmmov`: below this the sample is probably mostly stormwater
#   (heavy rain dilutes everything, see the March 2023 floods)
# * `blank_max_copies`: amplification in the extraction blank above this invalidates the *whole batch*, not just one sample


def apply_qc(df: pd.DataFrame, qc: dict) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Drop samples failing QC and return the filtered copy."""
    plant_median = df.groupby("plant")["bcov_cq"].transform("median")
    df = df.assign(
        cq_shift=(df["bcov_cq"] - plant_median).abs(),
        low_pmmov=df["pmmov_copies_l"] < qc["min_pmmov"],
    )
    bad_batches = df.loc[df["blank_copies"] > qc["blank_max_copies"], "batch"].unique()
    keep = (df["cq_shift"] <= qc["max_cq_shift"]) & ~df["low_pmmov"] & ~df["batch"].isin(bad_batches)
    log.info("QC: keeping %d of %d samples, %d batch(es) invalidated", keep.sum(), len(df), len(bad_batches))
    return df.loc[keep].copy()

    # N1 copies per PMMoV copy, times 1e6 so the numbers are readable
    df["n1_norm"] = df["n1_copies_l"] / df["pmmov_copies_l"] * 1e6
    df["log_n1_norm"] = np.log10(df["n1_norm"].clip(lower=1e-3))
    return df


def smooth(df, frac=0.3, it=1):
    out = []
    for plant, g in df.sort_values("sample_date").groupby("plant"):
        if len(g) < 3:
            log.warning("%s: only %d valid samples, not smoothing", plant, len(g))
            continue
        x = (g["sample_date"] - g["sample_date"].min()).dt.days.to_numpy()
        fit = lowess(g["log_n1_norm"], x, frac=frac, it=it, return_sorted=False)
        out.append(g.assign(trend=fit))
    return pd.concat(out)


def two_week_change(g):
    """Percent change of the smoothed, back-transformed level over the last 14 days."""
    last = g["sample_date"].max()
    now = g.loc[g["sample_date"] == last, "trend"].iloc[0]
    before = np.interp((last - pd.Timedelta(days=14)).value, g["sample_date"].astype("int64"), g["trend"])
    return 100 * (10 ** (now - before) - 1)


# fmt: markdown
CONFIG_HELP = """
Configuration
-------------

Pass `--config my.yaml` to override any of the defaults. Only the top-level keys you give are replaced; everything else keeps its default value.  A config for the two coastal plants, with the stricter QC we used during the 2023 floods, looks like this:

```yaml
plants: [ALV,  ESK]
qc:
    max_cq_shift: 1.5
    min_pmmov: 5.0e+05
    blank_max_copies: 0
smoothing: {frac: 0.25,it: 2}
```

Keys that are not recognised are ignored __silently__ (sorry).
"""

# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence
SUMMARY_TEMPLATE = """---
title: "Wastewater surveillance: week {week}"
author:    Environmental Epidemiology Unit
date: "{date}"
format:
    docx:
       reference-doc: templates/sitrep.docx
---

## Summary for week {week}

SARS-CoV-2 RNA in wastewater **{direction}** compared with the previous week at {n_up} of {n_plants} plants. The population-weighted trend changed by {pct_change:+.1f}% over the last 14 days. Plants with fewer than three valid samples in the window are not shown. See the methods annex for details of the normalisation, e.g. why PMMoV is used instead of flow-based normalisation.

Per-plant trends:

{plant_table}

_Prepared automatically by ww_pipeline.py -- please check the figures before circulating!_
"""

# %% [markdown]
# ## Load this week's data and apply QC

# %%
#| label: load
#| tbl-cap: "Valid samples per plant after QC"
def parse_args(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Weekly wastewater sitrep", epilog=CONFIG_HELP,
                                formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    p.add_argument("--week", default=pd.Timestamp.today().strftime("%G-W%V"))
    p.add_argument("--plants", nargs="+", default=None)
    p.add_argument("--config", type=Path)
    return p.parse_args(argv)

args = parse_args([] if "ipykernel" in sys.modules else None)
cfg = DEFAULT_CONFIG | (yaml.safe_load(args.config.read_text()) if args.config else {})
plants = args.plants or cfg["plants"]

raw = pd.concat(
    [pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / f"{p}_qpcr.csv", parse_dates=["sample_date"]).assign(plant=p) for p in plants],
    ignore_index=True,
)
clean = smooth(normalise(apply_qc(raw, cfg["qc"])), **cfg["smoothing"])
clean.groupby("plant").size().rename("n_valid").to_frame()

# %%
#| label: fig-trends
#| fig-cap: "Normalised N1 concentration (log10 copies per 10^6 PMMoV copies) with LOWESS trend, by treatment plant. Grey points are individual samples."
#| fig-height:  6
#| fig-width: 9
#| layout-ncol: 1
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(plants), 1, sharex=True, figsize=(9, 1.6 * len(plants)))
for ax, (plant, g) in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), clean.groupby("plant")):
    ax.scatter(g["sample_date"], g["log_n1_norm"], s=8, alpha=0.5, color="grey")
    ax.plot(g["sample_date"], g["trend"], lw=2)
    ax.set_ylabel(plant, rotation=0, ha="right")
fig.tight_layout()

# %%
#| label: write-outputs
#| output: false
#| tags: [outputs,   sitrep]
out_dir = RESULTS_DIR / args.week
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
clean.to_csv(out_dir / "clean_samples.csv", index=False)

changes = clean.groupby("plant").apply(two_week_change).rename("pct_change_14d")
weights = pd.Series(cfg["population"]).reindex(changes.index)
pooled = float(np.average(changes, weights=weights))

(out_dir / "summary.qmd").write_text(

        date=pd.Timestamp.today().date().isoformat(),
        direction="increased" if pooled > 0 else "decreased",
        n_up=int((changes > 0).sum()),
        n_plants=len(changes),
        pct_change=pooled,
        plant_table=changes.round(1).to_frame().to_markdown(),
    )
)
log.info("wrote %s", out_dir)

romsort

Sort, rename and de-duplicate your ROM dumps using [No-Intro](https://no-intro.org "No-Intro dat-o-matic") and [Redump][redump] DAT files. Everything happens locally, nothing gets uploaded anywhere, and it never deletes a file unless you explicitly pass `--delete-dupes` **and** confirm. I wrote this because my "Retro" folder had grown to 40 GB of `Super Mario World (USA) (1).zip`, `smw_final_FINAL.sfc` and friends, and every existing tool either wanted a GUI, Windows, or both. [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-mkdocs-blue)](https://kitokafor.github.io/romsort/) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/pypi/dm/romsort)](https://pypistats.org/packages/romsort) > **Note** > romsort only works with ROMs you dumped yourself or are otherwise legally allowed to have. It never downloads ROMs and never will, so please don't open issues asking for that. ## Features ## * Matches files by CRC32/SHA-1 against DAT files, so the filename doesn't matter at all * Renames to the canonical No-Intro / Redump name + Sorts into per-system folders (`snes/`, `megadrive/`, `psx/` ...) + **1G1R** mode: keeps one game per title, preferring your region order (`--regions EUR,USA,JPN`) - Handles `.zip` and `.7z` archives, and multi-track `.cue`/`.bin` sets - Dry-run by default :sunglasses: — you have to pass `--apply` to actually move anything Installation ------------ ```bash pipx install romsort # or, if you like living on the edge pipx install git+https://github.com/kitokafor/romsort ``` Needs Python 3.10 or newer. 7z support needs `py7zr`, which is an optional extra: `pipx install "romsort[7z]"`. ## Usage romsort scan ~/Roms/unsorted --dat-dir ~/Roms/dats romsort sort ~/Roms/unsorted ~/Roms/sorted --apply The first command only reads; it prints a report of what it found and what it *would* do. The second one actually moves files. Here's what the output looks like on a small folder: ~~~console $ romsort scan ./unsorted --dat-dir ./dats loaded 14 DAT files (38,212 entries) matched 212 / 230 files unknown 18 files (see romsort-unknown.txt) dupes 9 files (same SHA-1, different names) ~~~ ### Commands | command | what it does | safe? | |---|---|:---:| | `scan` | hash everything, match against the DATs, print a report | :white_check_mark: | | `sort` | move/rename matched files into `DEST//` | only with `--apply` | | `dedupe` | find duplicates, optionally delete them | :warning: with `--delete-dupes` | |`dat update`|download the latest DATs from your configured sources|:white_check_mark:| ### Config file romsort looks for `~/.config/romsort/config.yaml`. Every option can also be passed on the command line, the config file just saves typing. Files whose name ends in \_old or starts with \# are skipped, which is a leftover from my own folder structure and will probably become an option at some point. ```yaml # ~/.config/romsort/config.yaml dat_dir: ~/Roms/dats regions: [EUR, USA,JPN] one_game_one_rom: true systems: snes: {dat: "Nintendo - Super Nintendo Entertainment System", folder: snes} md: {dat: "Sega - Mega Drive - Genesis", folder: megadrive} psx: dat: Sony - PlayStation folder: psx prefer: [cue, chd] ignore: - "*.txt" - '*.nfo' - "[BIOS]*" ``` ## FAQ **Q: Why are some of my files "unknown"?** Usually one of these: 1) it's a bad dump or a hack (hacks aren't in No-Intro, by design) 2) it has a header the DAT doesn't expect. romsort strips iNES and SMC headers automatically, but not every weird copier header out there 3) you don't have the DAT for that system yet **Q: Can it convert `.bin`/`.cue` to `.chd`?**\ No, use `chdman` for that. romsort will happily sort the `.chd` files afterwards though. **Q: Does it work on Windows?** Probably? I don't have a Windows machine to test on. CI runs on Windows and the tests pass, which is about as much as I can promise. ## Roadmap - [x] No-Intro DATs - [x] Redump DATs (multi-track) - [ ] MAME (honestly, probably never, MAME sets are their own universe) - [ ] a tiny TUI for reviewing the "unknown" pile - [ ] with cover art from libretro-thumbnails? maybe ## Contributing PRs welcome! Please read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md "how to set up a dev environment") first, and run `make check` before pushing. If you're adding support for a new system, add a tiny *fake* DAT and fake ROM to `tests/fixtures/` (just a few bytes, __never__ real ROMs). *** Made with :heart: and too much coffee by Kit. Thanks to the [No-Intro][no-intro] and [Redump][redump] projects, without whom none of this would be possible, and to everyone who has ever filed a bug with a *useful* reproduction.[^1] ## License #### MIT, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). [^1]: you know who you are. there are four of you. [redump]: http://redump.org/ "Redump disc preservation" [no-intro]: https://no-intro.org

#' * **Visa VDMP** -- early warning at 0.65% of transactions *and* 75 disputes in a calendar month.
#' * **Mastercard ECM** -- 1.5% and 100 chargebacks; we warn at 1.2%.
#'     + excessive merchants are re-evaluated every month
#' * the internal watch list maintained by the risk desk (`risk.watchlist`)
#'
#' Ratios use the **previous** month's settled transaction count as the denominator, because that is how the schemes compute them.
thresholds <- tribble(
  ~scheme,      ~warn_ratio, ~warn_count, ~programme,
  "visa",       0.0065,      75,          "VDMP",
  "mastercard", 0.012,       100,         "ECM"
)

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn = "risk-warehouse", timeout = 30)
on.exit(dbDisconnect(con), add = TRUE)

lookback_start <- floor_date(today(), "month") %m-% months(13)

monthly <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT merchant_id, mcc, scheme, date_trunc('month', settled_at) AS month,
         count(*) AS txn_count,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE has_dispute) AS dispute_count
  FROM risk.card_transactions
  WHERE settled_at >= ?
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
", params = list(lookback_start)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(month = as_date(month))

flag_merchants <- function(monthly, thresholds, min_txn = 100) {
  # fmt: markdown
  # A merchant is flagged when **both** the ratio and the absolute count exceed the early-warning level of its scheme.   Months below `min_txn` settled transactions are ignored entirely; see *Thresholds* above for the numbers.
  monthly |>
    arrange(merchant_id, scheme, month) |>
    group_by(merchant_id, scheme) |>
    mutate(prev_txn = lag(txn_count), ratio = dispute_count / prev_txn) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(!is.na(prev_txn), prev_txn >= min_txn) |>
    inner_join(thresholds, by = "scheme") |>
    mutate(flagged = ratio >= warn_ratio & dispute_count >= warn_count)
}

current <- flags |> filter(month == max(month), flagged)

  ggplot(aes(month, ratio, colour = scheme)) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Dispute ratio", colour = "Scheme")

output_path <- glue("s3://acme-risk-reports/chargebacks/{week_label}/flags.parquet")
write_parquet(current, output_path)

previous <- read_parquet(glue("s3://acme-risk-reports/chargebacks/{format(today() - 7, '%G-W%V')}/flags.parquet"))

summary_template <- r"(
### Chargeback monitor -- week {week_label}

{n_flagged} merchants crossed an early-warning threshold this week, {n_new} of them for the first time.  Merchants that are already in a scheme programme are listed separately in the attached workbook.
1) Review the new merchants with their account managers before **Thursday**.
2) For repeat offenders, check whether the remediation plan agreed last month is actually being followed.
+ Raw data: `{output_path}`
)"

# fmt: markdown
footer_md <- "
---
_This report is generated automatically by `chargeback_monitor.R`. Numbers are preliminary until the acquirer files for the month are final, which is usually the case by the 6th business day._
"

# Adaptive Card skeleton for the risk channel; the text block is filled in below.
# fmt: json
teams_card <- r"(
{"type": "message", "attachments": [{"contentType": "application/vnd.microsoft.card.adaptive",
  "content": {"type": "AdaptiveCard", "version": "1.5", "body": [{"type": "TextBlock", "text": "", "wrap": true}]}}]}
)"

message_md <- paste0(
  report_intro,
  glue(summary_template, n_flagged = nrow(current)),
  footer_md
)

card <- jsonlite::fromJSON(teams_card, simplifyVector = FALSE)
card$attachments[[1]]$content$body[[1]]$text <- message_md

if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("RISK_TEAMS_WEBHOOK"))) {
  httr2::request(Sys.getenv("RISK_TEAMS_WEBHOOK")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(card, auto_unbox = TRUE) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    httr2::req_perform()
} else {
  cat(message_md, sep = "\n")
}

ggsave(glue("output/dispute-trend-{week_label}.png"), p_trend, width = 9, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)

---
title:  "Drought shocks and school enrolment in rural Ethiopia"
subtitle: 'Evidence from the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey, 2011–2016'
author:

date: last-modified
date-format: "D MMMM YYYY"
abstract: "We combine three waves of the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey (ESS) with gridded rainfall data to estimate how drought shocks affect primary school enrolment. A one standard deviation shortfall in growing-season rainfall reduces enrolment of children aged 7–14 by about 3 percentage points, with larger effects for girls and for households that do not receive transfers from the Productive Safety Net Programme."
keywords: [drought, education,  "human capital", Ethiopia,panel data]
bibliography: references.bib

    geometry: ["margin=2.5cm", "a4paper"]
    keep-tex: true
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        \usepackage{booktabs}
        \usepackage{siunitx}
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
crossref:
  fig-prefix: Figure
  tbl-prefix:   Table
  eq-prefix: Equation

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(modelsummary)
library(sf)

panel  <- read_rds(here::here("data", "ess_panel_children.rds"))
kebele <- read_rds(here::here("data", "spi3_kebele.rds"))
n_hh   <- n_distinct(panel$household_id)
```

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Ethiopia's agricultural economy remains highly exposed to rainfall variability: roughly 85% of households depend on rain-fed crop production, and the 2015/16 El Niño drought was the worst in fifty years [@fews2016; @dercon2004, p. 312]. A large literature documents the consequences of such shocks for consumption and child nutrition [@dercon2005; @hoddinott2006], but the evidence on schooling is mixed. Children may be withdrawn from school to work on the farm or to save on fees, or, conversely, enrolment may *increase* in a bad year because the opportunity cost of children's time falls [@jacoby1997; @shah2017].

This paper uses three waves of the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey (ESS) to estimate the effect of growing-season rainfall shocks on primary school enrolment. Our sample contains `r nrow(panel)` child-year observations from `{r} n_hh` households. We find that drought reduces enrolment, and that the effect is concentrated among girls and among households outside the Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP)[^psnp].

[^psnp]: The PSNP is a public works and cash/food transfer programme introduced in 2005. It currently covers around 8 million people in chronically food-insecure woredas; see @gilligan2009 for an early evaluation of its effects on food security and asset accumulation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Replication material
All code is in the `analysis/` folder of the replication package. The ESS microdata cannot be redistributed, but can be downloaded free of charge from the [World Bank Microdata Library](https://microdata.worldbank.org/index.php/catalog/lsms "LSMS-ISA catalogue") after registration. Run `targets::tar_make()` to rebuild everything.
:::

## Data {#sec-data}

### Survey data

The ESS is part of the Living Standards Measurement Study -- Integrated Surveys on Agriculture (LSMS-ISA). We use the 2011/12, 2013/14 and 2015/16 waves, which follow the same rural households. The outcome is a dummy for current enrolment of children aged 7--14 at the time of the interview.

### Rainfall

Rainfall comes from CHIRPS v2.0 [@funk2015], a 0.05° gridded product blending satellite estimates with station data. For each kebele we compute the Standardised Precipitation Index for the *kiremt* (main rainy) season, June to September:

$$
\text{SPI}_{kt} = \Phi^{-1}\!\left( G_k(R_{kt}) \right)
$$ {#eq-spi}

where $G_k$ is the gamma distribution fitted to 1981–2010 kiremt rainfall in kebele $k$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. Following convention, a season with $\text{SPI}_{kt} < -1$ counts as a drought.

![Kiremt SPI by kebele in 2015. Darker colours are drier; dots mark ESS enumeration areas.](figures/spi_map_2015.png){#fig-map fig-alt="Choropleth map of Ethiopia showing the standardised precipitation index for the 2015 kiremt season, with the driest areas in the north-east (Afar and eastern Amhara) and enumeration areas shown as black dots." width="80%"}

@fig-map shows that the 2015 drought was concentrated in the north-east, in Afar, eastern Amhara and parts of Oromia, i.e. in areas where the PSNP was already active.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-balance
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics by drought exposure, pooled sample"
#| tbl-colwidths: [40,20,20,20]
panel |>
  mutate(drought = if_else(spi3 < -1, "Drought", "No drought")) |>
  select(drought, enrolled, age, female, hh_size, head_female, log_cons, psnp) |>
  datasummary_balance(~drought, data = _, dinm = TRUE, fmt = 3)
```

@tbl-balance compares children in kebeles with and without a drought in the survey year. Drought-affected households are poorer and more likely to be PSNP beneficiaries, which is why all specifications include child fixed effects.

## Empirical strategy

We estimate a linear probability model with child and region-by-year fixed effects:

$$
E_{ikt} = \beta\,\text{SPI}_{kt} + \gamma' X_{ikt} + \alpha_i + \delta_{r(k)t} + \varepsilon_{ikt}
$$ {#eq-main}

Standard errors are clustered by kebele, the level at which the shock varies [@abadie2023]. The key terms are defined as follows.

Drought
:   A kiremt season with $\text{SPI}_{kt} < -1$, i.e. roughly the driest 16% of seasons in the reference period.

PSNP household
: A household that reported receiving PSNP transfers (cash or food) in the 12 months before the interview.  Public works participants and direct-support beneficiaries are pooled.

Enrolled
:  The child currently attends primary or lower-secondary school according to the household roster. We do not observe actual attendance, which probably responds more strongly to shocks than enrolment does.

## Results

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Pooled

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Effect of rainfall shocks on enrolment (linear probability model)"
models <- list(
  "(1)" = feols(enrolled ~ spi3 | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id),
  "(2)" = feols(enrolled ~ spi3 + hh_size + head_female + log_cons | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id),
  "(3)" = feols(enrolled ~ drought | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id)
)
modelsummary(models, stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared.within"))
```

### By sex and PSNP status

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Effect of a one-SD rainfall shortfall on enrolment by subgroup, with 95% confidence intervals."}
het <- feols(enrolled ~ spi3 | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id, split = ~interaction(female, psnp))
coefplot(het)
```

### Robustness

1. Dropping the 2015/16 wave, in which attrition was highest.
2. Using the continuous rainfall deviation in mm instead of the SPI.
3. Adding woreda-specific linear trends.
4. Restricting the sample to children who were enrolled in the first wave.

All four leave the main coefficient between [-0.034 and -0.026]{.mark}; see Appendix A.

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-event
#| fig-cap: "Enrolment around the 2015 drought"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Drought-affected kebeles"
#|   - 'Other kebeles'
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts of enrolment rates by survey wave. Enrolment falls in 2015/16 in drought-affected kebeles but not elsewhere."
for (g in c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
  p <- panel |> filter(drought_2015 == g) |> count(wave, wt = enrolled / n()) |> ggplot(aes(wave, n)) + geom_line() + geom_point()
  print(p)
}
```

The estimates in @tbl-main imply that a one-SD shortfall reduces enrolment by about 3 percentage points, roughly a tenth of the gap between the poorest and richest consumption quintile. @fig-event suggests that this is not driven by pre-existing trends.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Attrition
About 9% of the households interviewed in 2011/12 could not be re-interviewed in 2015/16, and attrition was higher in drought-affected zones. If the households that left were those hit hardest, our estimates are biased towards zero. Bounds following @lee2009 are reported in Appendix B[^bounds].
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
Girls' enrolment drops by 4.1 percentage points, boys' by 1.9. The difference is significant at the 5% level, consistent with households protecting the education of the child with the higher expected labour market return [cf. @jensen2010].
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
> "When the rains failed, my daughter stayed home to fetch water."
>
> --- Mother of three, South Wollo (qualitative module, 2016)
:::

::::

## Conclusion

Rainfall shocks have measurable consequences for human capital accumulation in rural Ethiopia, and the PSNP appears to shield households from the worst of them. Expanding social protection *before* a drought is declared, rather than after, would likely protect enrolment as well as consumption.

[^bounds]: Lee bounds trim the distribution of the outcome in the group with lower attrition; because our outcome is binary, the bounds are wide but still exclude zero for girls.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

  mutate(drought = if_else(spi3 < -1, "Drought", "No drought")) |>
  select(drought, enrolled, age, female, hh_size, head_female, log_cons, psnp) |>
  datasummary_balance(~drought, data = _, dinm = TRUE, fmt = 3)
```

@tbl-balance compares children in kebeles with and without a drought in the survey year. Drought-affected households are poorer and more likely to be PSNP beneficiaries, which is why all specifications include child fixed effects.

## Empirical strategy

We estimate a linear probability model with child and region-by-year fixed effects:

$$
E_{ikt} = \beta\,\text{SPI}_{kt} + \gamma' X_{ikt} + \alpha_i + \delta_{r(k)t} + \varepsilon_{ikt}
$$ {#eq-main}

Standard errors are clustered by kebele, the level at which the shock varies [@abadie2023]. The key terms are defined as follows.

Drought
:   A kiremt season with $\text{SPI}_{kt} < -1$, i.e. roughly the driest 16% of seasons in the reference period.

PSNP household
: A household that reported receiving PSNP transfers (cash or food) in the 12 months before the interview.  Public works participants and direct-support beneficiaries are pooled.

Enrolled
:  The child currently attends primary or lower-secondary school according to the household roster. We do not observe actual attendance, which probably responds more strongly to shocks than enrolment does.

## Results

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Pooled

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Effect of rainfall shocks on enrolment (linear probability model)"
models <- list(
  "(1)" = feols(enrolled ~ spi3 | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id),
  "(2)" = feols(enrolled ~ spi3 + hh_size + head_female + log_cons | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id),
  "(3)" = feols(enrolled ~ drought | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id)
)
modelsummary(models, stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared.within"))
```

### By sex and PSNP status

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Effect of a one-SD rainfall shortfall on enrolment by subgroup, with 95% confidence intervals."}
het <- feols(enrolled ~ spi3 | child_id + region^year, data = panel, cluster = ~kebele_id, split = ~interaction(female, psnp))
coefplot(het)
```

### Robustness

1. Dropping the 2015/16 wave, in which attrition was highest.
2. Using the continuous rainfall deviation in mm instead of the SPI.
3. Adding woreda-specific linear trends.
4. Restricting the sample to children who were enrolled in the first wave.

All four leave the main coefficient between [-0.034 and -0.026]{.mark}; see Appendix A.

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-event
#| fig-cap: "Enrolment around the 2015 drought"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Drought-affected kebeles"
#|   - 'Other kebeles'
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts of enrolment rates by survey wave. Enrolment falls in 2015/16 in drought-affected kebeles but not elsewhere."
for (g in c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
  p <- panel |> filter(drought_2015 == g) |> count(wave, wt = enrolled / n()) |> ggplot(aes(wave, n)) + geom_line() + geom_point()
  print(p)
}
```

The estimates in @tbl-main imply that a one-SD shortfall reduces enrolment by about 3 percentage points, roughly a tenth of the gap between the poorest and richest consumption quintile. @fig-event suggests that this is not driven by pre-existing trends.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Attrition
About 9% of the households interviewed in 2011/12 could not be re-interviewed in 2015/16, and attrition was higher in drought-affected zones. If the households that left were those hit hardest, our estimates are biased towards zero. Bounds following @lee2009 are reported in Appendix B[^bounds].
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
Girls' enrolment drops by 4.1 percentage points, boys' by 1.9. The difference is significant at the 5% level, consistent with households protecting the education of the child with the higher expected labour market return [cf. @jensen2010].
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
> "When the rains failed, my daughter stayed home to fetch water."
>
> --- Mother of three, South Wollo (qualitative module, 2016)
:::

::::

## Conclusion

Rainfall shocks have measurable consequences for human capital accumulation in rural Ethiopia, and the PSNP appears to shield households from the worst of them. Expanding social protection *before* a drought is declared, rather than after, would likely protect enrolment as well as consumption.

[^bounds]: Lee bounds trim the distribution of the outcome in the group with lower attrition; because our outcome is binary, the bounds are wide but still exclude zero for girls.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::
