kiln

A fast, cross-platform task runner that reads plain TOML and gets out of your way.
Think make without the tabs, or npm run without the node_modules.

[![CI](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/kiln-cli.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/kiln-cli) [![Homebrew](https://img.shields.io/homebrew/v/kiln)](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/kiln) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/kiln-rs/kiln/total.svg)](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1029384756193847296?label=discord&logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/kiln-rs) --- ## Table of Contents - [Features](#features) - [Installation](#installation) - [Homebrew (macOS / Linux)](#homebrew-macos--linux) - [Scoop (Windows)](#scoop-windows) - [Cargo](#cargo) - [Prebuilt binaries](#prebuilt-binaries) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Options](#options) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Contributors](#contributors) - [License](#license) ## Features * ⚡ **Fast.** kiln is a single static binary written in Rust; `kiln --version` returns in under 2 ms on a cold cache. * 📄 **Plain TOML** – no DSL to learn, no significant whitespace, no tabs-vs-spaces holy wars. * 🔗 **Task dependencies** with automatic parallelism: independent tasks run concurrently, up to `--jobs` at a time. * 🧠 *Content-addressed caching* — declare `inputs` and `outputs` and kiln skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed (hashes, not mtimes). - 🪟 __First-class Windows support__. Yes, really: `cmd.exe`, PowerShell and Git Bash are all tested in CI. - 👀 `kiln watch` re-runs tasks when files change, with debouncing and `.gitignore` support - 🐚 Shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell and elvish * 🎨 Pretty, _colorized_ output that degrades gracefully when piped (and respects [`NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org)) ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS / Linux) ```sh brew install kiln ``` ### Scoop (Windows) ```powershell scoop bucket add extras scoop install extras/kiln ``` ### Cargo If you already have a Rust toolchain (**1.74 or newer**): ```sh cargo install kiln-cli --locked ``` > **Note:** the crate is called `kiln-cli` because `kiln` was already taken on crates.io by an unrelated (and long-abandoned) project. The installed binary is still just `kiln`. ### Prebuilt binaries Grab the archive for your platform from the [latest release](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases/latest), unpack it, and drop the `kiln` binary somewhere on your `PATH`. Every archive ships with a `.sha256` checksum next to it. | Platform | Arch | Archive | Notes | |----------|:----:|---------|-------| | Linux | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | statically linked, works on Alpine | | Linux | aarch64 | `kiln-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | Raspberry Pi 4/5, AWS Graviton | | macOS | Apple Silicon | `kiln-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | signed & notarized | | macOS | Intel | `kiln-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | | | Windows | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` | needs the VC++ 2015–2022 redistributable | | FreeBSD | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-freebsd.tar.gz` | community maintained, best effort | ## Quick start Create a `kiln.toml` at the root of your project: ```toml [tasks.build] run = "cargo build --release" [tasks.test] run = "cargo test --all-features" deps = ["build"] ``` Run a task (its dependencies run first): ```console $ kiln test ``` ``` ▸ build cargo build --release Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.21s ▸ test cargo test --all-features Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/demo-3f1c2a9b) test result: ok. 42 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out ✔ 2 tasks finished in 3.48s (1 cached) ``` List what's available: ```console $ kiln --list build cargo build --release test cargo test --all-features (deps: build) ``` ## Configuration kiln looks for `kiln.toml` in the current directory and then walks up towards the filesystem root, stopping at the first one it finds (or at a directory containing `.git`). Point it somewhere else with `--file path/to/kiln.toml` or the `KILN_FILE` environment variable. ```toml [settings] shell = "bash" # "sh", "bash", "zsh", "pwsh" or "cmd" jobs = 4 dotenv = [".env", ".env.local"] [tasks.fmt] description = "Format Rust and TypeScript sources" run = ["cargo fmt --all", "npx prettier --write 'web/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}'"] [tasks.web] dir = "web" run = "npm run dev" inputs = ["src/**/*", "package.json"] outputs = ["dist/**"] ``` ### Options | Key | Type | Default | Description | |-----|------|---------|-------------| | `settings.shell` | string | `"sh"` on Unix, `"cmd"` on Windows | The shell used to execute `run` commands. Each command is handed to the shell as a single string, so pipes, redirects, globbing and `&&` behave exactly as they would in your terminal. | | `settings.jobs` | integer | number of logical CPUs | Upper bound on how many tasks may run concurrently. Set it to `1` to force sequential execution, which is handy when debugging an ordering problem or when two tasks fight over the same port. | | `settings.dotenv` | array of strings | `[]` | Files to load environment variables from, in order; later files override earlier ones. Missing files are silently skipped, so it's safe to list `.env.local` even if most people on the team don't have one. | | `settings.color` | string | `"auto"` | Whether to emit ANSI colors. `auto` enables them only when stdout is a TTY and `NO_COLOR` is unset. | | `tasks..run` | string \| array | — (required) | Command(s) to execute. When an array is given the commands run one after another in the same working directory, and the task fails as soon as one of them exits non-zero. | | `tasks..deps` | array of strings | `[]` | Tasks that must finish successfully before this one starts. Cycles are detected at load time and reported with the full path, e.g. `a -> b -> c -> a`. | | `tasks..inputs` / `outputs` | array of globs | `[]` | Used for caching. If none of the files matched by `inputs` changed since the last successful run *and* every `outputs` glob still matches at least one file, the task is skipped and reported as `cached`. | | `tasks..dir` | string | directory of `kiln.toml` | Working directory for the task, relative to the config file. | Every setting can also be overridden from the environment: `KILN_JOBS`, `KILN_SHELL`, `KILN_COLOR`. Set `KILN_LOG=debug` to print the resolved task graph and every cache decision — it's the first thing we'll ask for in a bug report :wink: ## FAQ
How is this different from make? `make` is a build system that people (ab)use as a task runner. It's great at what it was designed for, but `.PHONY` targets, mandatory tabs, and the subtle differences between GNU make, BSD make and whatever ships with Xcode get old fast. kiln only does the task-runner part, and does it the same way on every OS.
Can I use kiln in a monorepo? Yes. Put a `kiln.toml` in each package and add `include = ["packages/*/kiln.toml"]` to the root file. Included tasks are namespaced by directory, e.g. `kiln api:test`.
Why TOML and not YAML? Because `on: yes` should not be a boolean. Also, kiln configs are short enough that YAML's extra features don't pull their weight.
## Contributors kiln wouldn't exist without [everyone who has contributed](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/graphs/contributors). Thank you! 💛 Want to help out? Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and look for issues labelled [`good first issue`](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22). ## License Licensed under either of * Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or ) * MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or ) at your option. Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in kiln by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# aligna

[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Tests](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8XK2M1P0Z)](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna)
[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/aligna/badge/?version=latest)](https://aligna.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)
[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/aligna.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/aligna)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.8812345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8812345)

**aligna** is a small, fast library for aligning time series — dynamic time warping (DTW), soft-DTW and a handful of related tools — with a NumPy-first API and optional PyTorch and JAX backends for when you need gradients.

It is used in production for speech keyword spotting, gait analysis and industrial sensor monitoring, and at least once that we know of for comparing the songs of humpback whales. 🐋

## Highlights

* Exact DTW with Sakoe–Chiba and Itakura constraints, arbitrary step patterns and early abandoning
* Soft-DTW and its gradient, on CPU or GPU
- Pairwise distance matrices for *ragged* collections (series of different lengths), parallelised with threads
- DTW barycenter averaging (DBA)
* Zero required dependencies beyond NumPy; Numba, PyTorch and JAX are picked up automatically if installed

## Concepts

Two time series rarely line up exactly. A person saying the same word twice will stretch some syllables and rush others; a machine going through the same duty cycle will idle a little longer one day than the next. Comparing such sequences point by point, with the Euclidean distance say, punishes these harmless shifts in timing just as heavily as genuine differences in shape. **Dynamic time warping** fixes this by finding the cheapest *monotonic* alignment between the two sequences — a path through the matrix of pairwise distances that may repeat elements of either series but never goes backwards in time — and reporting the total cost along that path.

The cost of exact DTW is quadratic in the length of the series, which is fine for a few thousand samples and painful beyond that. In practice you almost always want a _global constraint_: the Sakoe–Chiba band keeps the path within a fixed radius of the diagonal, while the Itakura parallelogram limits its slope. Both make the computation roughly linear in the series length and, as a pleasant side effect, prevent pathological alignments in which a single point of `x` is matched to half of `y`.

Classic DTW takes a hard minimum at every step, so it is not differentiable. *Soft-DTW* (Cuturi & Blondel, 2017) replaces that minimum with a smoothed soft-min controlled by a temperature `gamma`; as `gamma → 0` it recovers ordinary DTW, and for `gamma > 0` it has well-defined gradients everywhere. That makes it usable as a loss function for networks that output sequences, or for computing barycenters ("averages") of a set of series by gradient descent.

aligna implements all three ideas behind the same API, so you can prototype with plain NumPy arrays and switch to `aligna.torch` once you want to backpropagate through the alignment. 

## Installation

```bash
pip install aligna

# with the optional backends
pip install "aligna[torch]"     # PyTorch >= 2.1
pip install "aligna[jax]"       # JAX >= 0.4.20

# or from conda-forge
conda install -c conda-forge aligna
```

aligna requires Python 3.9+ and NumPy 1.23+. If [Numba](https://numba.pydata.org/) is installed it is used automatically, which gives a 10–40× speed-up on the CPU code paths.

## Quick tour

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import aligna
>>> x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> y = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y)
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.path[:5]
[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
>>> float(np.linalg.norm(x - y[:6]))  # point-by-point comparison is not zero
2.8284271247461903
```

Adding a global constraint is a single keyword argument:

```python
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y, window=aligna.SakoeChiba(radius=2))
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.normalized_distance   # distance / (len(x) + len(y))
0.0
```

Soft-DTW as a differentiable loss:

```python
>>> import torch
>>> from aligna.torch import soft_dtw
>>> pred = torch.randn(8, 50, 3, requires_grad=True)   # (batch, time, features)
>>> target = torch.randn(8, 64, 3)
>>> loss = soft_dtw(pred, target, gamma=0.1).mean()
>>> loss.backward()
>>> pred.grad.shape
torch.Size([8, 50, 3])
```

Pairwise distances between series of different lengths:

```python
>>> series = [np.sin(np.linspace(0, k, 80 + 10 * k)) for k in range(1, 6)]
>>> D = aligna.cdist(series, metric="dtw", window=aligna.SakoeChiba(10), n_jobs=-1)
>>> D.shape
(5, 5)
>>> bool(np.allclose(D, D.T)) and bool(np.all(np.diag(D) == 0))
True
```


## API overview

| Name | What it does | Backends |
|------|--------------|----------|
| `aligna.dtw(x, y, *, window=None, step="symmetric2", dist="sqeuclidean")` | Exact DTW. Returns a `DTWResult` with `.distance`, `.normalized_distance`, `.path` and, if requested, `.cost_matrix` | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.soft_dtw(x, y, gamma=1.0)` | Smoothed, differentiable DTW | NumPy, PyTorch, JAX |
| `aligna.cdist(X, Y=None, *, metric="dtw", n_jobs=1, **kw)` | Pairwise distance matrix between two collections of (possibly ragged) series | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.barycenter(series, method="dba", max_iter=30)` | DTW Barycenter Averaging, or soft-DTW barycenters with `method="soft"` | NumPy, PyTorch |
| `aligna.SakoeChiba(radius)`, `aligna.Itakura(max_slope)` | Global constraint windows | – |
| `aligna.steps` | Predefined step patterns: `symmetric1`, `symmetric2`, `asymmetric`, `rabinerJuang(...)` | – |
| `aligna.plot.alignment(x, y, path, ax=None)` | Quick matplotlib plot of two series and their warping path | – |

Full reference documentation lives at **[aligna.readthedocs.io](https://aligna.readthedocs.io)**.

## Comparison with alternatives

| | aligna | tslearn | dtaidistance | dtw-python | fastdtw |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Exact DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (approximate) |
| Soft-DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| GPU / autograd | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Multivariate series | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Custom step patterns | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Ragged inputs to `cdist` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Wheels, no compiler needed | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Classification / clustering models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (clustering only) | ❌ | ❌ |

This table reflects our best understanding as of aligna 0.9 (March 2026). [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)
[![Tests](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8XK2M1P0Z)](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna)
[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/aligna/badge/?version=latest)](https://aligna.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)
[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/aligna.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/aligna)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.8812345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8812345)

**aligna** is a small, fast library for aligning time series — dynamic time warping (DTW), soft-DTW and a handful of related tools — with a NumPy-first API and optional PyTorch and JAX backends for when you need gradients.

It is used in production for speech keyword spotting, gait analysis and industrial sensor monitoring, and at least once that we know of for comparing the songs of humpback whales. 🐋

## Highlights

* Exact DTW with Sakoe–Chiba and Itakura constraints, arbitrary step patterns and early abandoning
* Soft-DTW and its gradient, on CPU or GPU
- Pairwise distance matrices for *ragged* collections (series of different lengths), parallelised with threads
- DTW barycenter averaging (DBA)
* Zero required dependencies beyond NumPy; Numba, PyTorch and JAX are picked up automatically if installed

## Concepts

Two time series rarely line up exactly. A person saying the same word twice will stretch some syllables and rush others; a machine going through the same duty cycle will idle a little longer one day than the next. Comparing such sequences point by point, with the Euclidean distance say, punishes these harmless shifts in timing just as heavily as genuine differences in shape. **Dynamic time warping** fixes this by finding the cheapest *monotonic* alignment between the two sequences — a path through the matrix of pairwise distances that may repeat elements of either series but never goes backwards in time — and reporting the total cost along that path.

The cost of exact DTW is quadratic in the length of the series, which is fine for a few thousand samples and painful beyond that. In practice you almost always want a _global constraint_: the Sakoe–Chiba band keeps the path within a fixed radius of the diagonal, while the Itakura parallelogram limits its slope. Both make the computation roughly linear in the series length and, as a pleasant side effect, prevent pathological alignments in which a single point of `x` is matched to half of `y`.

Classic DTW takes a hard minimum at every step, so it is not differentiable. *Soft-DTW* (Cuturi & Blondel, 2017) replaces that minimum with a smoothed soft-min controlled by a temperature `gamma`; as `gamma → 0` it recovers ordinary DTW, and for `gamma > 0` it has well-defined gradients everywhere. That makes it usable as a loss function for networks that output sequences, or for computing barycenters ("averages") of a set of series by gradient descent.

aligna implements all three ideas behind the same API, so you can prototype with plain NumPy arrays and switch to `aligna.torch` once you want to backpropagate through the alignment. 

## Installation

```bash
pip install aligna

# with the optional backends
pip install "aligna[torch]"     # PyTorch >= 2.1
pip install "aligna[jax]"       # JAX >= 0.4.20

# or from conda-forge
conda install -c conda-forge aligna
```

aligna requires Python 3.9+ and NumPy 1.23+. If [Numba](https://numba.pydata.org/) is installed it is used automatically, which gives a 10–40× speed-up on the CPU code paths.

## Quick tour

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import aligna
>>> x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> y = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y)
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.path[:5]
[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
>>> float(np.linalg.norm(x - y[:6]))  # point-by-point comparison is not zero
2.8284271247461903
```

Adding a global constraint is a single keyword argument:

```python
>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y, window=aligna.SakoeChiba(radius=2))
>>> res.distance
0.0
>>> res.normalized_distance   # distance / (len(x) + len(y))
0.0
```

Soft-DTW as a differentiable loss:

```python
>>> import torch
>>> from aligna.torch import soft_dtw
>>> pred = torch.randn(8, 50, 3, requires_grad=True)   # (batch, time, features)
>>> target = torch.randn(8, 64, 3)
>>> loss = soft_dtw(pred, target, gamma=0.1).mean()
>>> loss.backward()
>>> pred.grad.shape
torch.Size([8, 50, 3])
```

```python
>>> series = [np.sin(np.linspace(0, k, 80 + 10 * k)) for k in range(1, 6)]
>>> D = aligna.cdist(series, metric="dtw", window=aligna.SakoeChiba(10), n_jobs=-1)
>>> D.shape
(5, 5)
>>> bool(np.allclose(D, D.T)) and bool(np.all(np.diag(D) == 0))
True
```


## API overview

| Name | What it does | Backends |
|------|--------------|----------|
| `aligna.dtw(x, y, *, window=None, step="symmetric2", dist="sqeuclidean")` | Exact DTW. Returns a `DTWResult` with `.distance`, `.normalized_distance`, `.path` and, if requested, `.cost_matrix` | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.soft_dtw(x, y, gamma=1.0)` | Smoothed, differentiable DTW | NumPy, PyTorch, JAX |
| `aligna.cdist(X, Y=None, *, metric="dtw", n_jobs=1, **kw)` | Pairwise distance matrix between two collections of (possibly ragged) series | NumPy, Numba |
| `aligna.barycenter(series, method="dba", max_iter=30)` | DTW Barycenter Averaging, or soft-DTW barycenters with `method="soft"` | NumPy, PyTorch |
| `aligna.SakoeChiba(radius)`, `aligna.Itakura(max_slope)` | Global constraint windows | – |
| `aligna.steps` | Predefined step patterns: `symmetric1`, `symmetric2`, `asymmetric`, `rabinerJuang(...)` | – |
| `aligna.plot.alignment(x, y, path, ax=None)` | Quick matplotlib plot of two series and their warping path | – |

Full reference documentation lives at **[aligna.readthedocs.io](https://aligna.readthedocs.io)**.

| Classification / clustering models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (clustering only) | ❌ | ❌ |

# Changelog

All notable changes to Brisk will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

### Added
- `app.route()` now accepts a `RouteGroup`, so nested routers can share middleware without re-declaring it ([#2291](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2291))

### Fixed
- Streaming responses no longer buffer the first chunk when compression is enabled ([#2302](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2302))

## [4.2.0] - 2026-10-28

### Added
- First-class Web Streams support for request bodies: `ctx.req.body` is a `ReadableStream` when `bodyParser: false` is set ([#2240](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2240))
- New `@brisk/otel` package with OpenTelemetry tracing middleware ([#2251](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2251))
  - Spans are named after the matched route pattern (`GET /users/:id`) rather than the raw URL, to keep cardinality low
  - Honours the standard `OTEL_*` environment variables
  - Propagates W3C `traceparent` headers by default
- `ctx.json()` accepts a `status` option, e.g. `ctx.json(user, { status: 201 })`

### Changed
- The default `maxBodySize` was raised from `1mb` to `4mb` to match common reverse-proxy defaults ([#2238](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2238))
- Route matching is ~18% faster on large route tables thanks to a radix-tree rewrite by @mkowalczyk ([#2219](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2219))

### Deprecated
- `ctx.request` is deprecated in favour of `ctx.req` and will be removed in 5.0. A one-time warning is logged in development.

### Fixed
- Multiple `Set-Cookie` headers were joined with a comma instead of being sent separately ([#2244](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2244))
- Fixed a crash in `serveStatic()` on Windows when the request path contained an encoded backslash (`%5C`)

## [4.1.1] - 2026-09-15

### Fixed
* Type inference for route params broke when a path contained a regex segment like `/:id(\\d+)` ([#2231](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2231))
* `brisk dev` no longer leaks a file watcher on every reload 

### Security
* Upgraded `path-to-regexp` to address a ReDoS with two parameters in a single segment (e.g. `/:a-:b`). Upgrading is **strongly** recommended if you accept user-defined routes.

## [4.1.0] - 2026-08-30

### Added
- `app.onError()` hooks can now be async
- The CORS middleware accepts a function for `origin`: `cors({ origin: (o) => o.endsWith(".example.com") })` ([#2201](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2201))
- Experimental Bun adapter, `@brisk/adapter-bun` — _please_ report issues!

### Changed
- `ctx.redirect()` now defaults to `302` instead of `301`. Permanent redirects are cached aggressively by browsers, which surprised a lot of people ([#2188](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2188))

### Fixed
- `HEAD` requests to routes that only define `GET` now return the correct `Content-Length`

## [4.0.0] - 2026-07-01

This is a major release. The headline changes are that Brisk is now ESM-only and requires Node.js 22 or later.

### Migration notes

Most applications can upgrade by replacing `require("brisk")` with `import { createApp } from "brisk"` and bumping their Node.js version. If you wrote custom middleware against the 3.x `(req, res, next)` signature, wrap it with `fromConnect()` from `@brisk/compat`, which adapts Connect/Express-style middleware to the new `(ctx, next)` model at a small performance cost; we recommend porting hot-path middleware by hand. The `config/` directory convention is gone — pass options to `createApp()` directly or load them with your favourite config library. The [upgrade guide](https://brisk.dev/docs/upgrading/v4) has a full checklist, and `npx @brisk/codemod v4 ./src` automates most of the mechanical changes.

### Added
- `(ctx, next)` middleware signature with full type inference for `ctx.state`
- Built-in request validation via [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so it works with Zod, Valibot and ArkType
- `brisk routes` CLI command that prints the route table

### Changed
- **BREAKING:** ESM-only; the CommonJS build has been removed ([#2050](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2050))
- **BREAKING:** the minimum supported Node.js version is now 22.
- **BREAKING:** the `ctx.body` setter is replaced by explicit helpers:
  - `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()` and `ctx.html()` for buffered responses
  - `ctx.stream()` for streaming
  - `ctx.empty(status)` for `204`/`304`

### Removed
- The `brisk/legacy` entry point
- The `app.listen(port, callback)` overload — use `await app.listen({ port })`
- Support for the `config/` directory convention

## [3.9.2] - 2026-05-19

### Fixed
- Memory leak when a client aborted a request while a `ctx.stream()` was pending ([#2011](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2011))

### Security
- Session cookies now default to `SameSite=Lax` (previously the attribute was not set at all)
- `serveStatic()` rejects paths containing null bytes


## [3.9.1] - 2026-04-02

### Fixed
* Regression in 3.9.0 where trailing slashes were stripped from mounted sub-app paths
    * `/admin/` returned 404 when the sub-app was mounted at `/admin`
    * strict mode (`strictSlash: true`) was not affected

## [3.9.0] - 2026-03-21

### Added
- `ctx.signal`, an `AbortSignal` that fires when the client disconnects
- Per-route `timeout` option

### Deprecated
- The `(req, res, next)` middleware signature. It keeps working in 3.x, but 4.0 will require `@brisk/compat` ([#1974](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/1974))
- `app.listen(port, callback)`

### Fixed
- Query strings with repeated keys (`?tag=a&tag=b`) are now consistently parsed into arrays

## [3.8.0] - 2026-01-12

### Added
- HTTP/2 support behind the `http2: true` option ([#1902](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/1902))
- `ctx.cookies.getAll()`

### Changed
- Development error pages now show the source snippet and a clickable stack trace
  - set `BRISK_ERROR_OVERLAY=0` to turn this off

### Removed
- Support for Node.js 16, which has been end-of-life for well over two years

## [3.7.1] - 2025-11-30

### Fixed
- `ETag` generation for empty bodies
- Typo in the default `X-Content-Type-Options` header (`nosnif` → `nosniff`) 🤦

### Security
- Bumped `cookie` to 0.7.2 to reject out-of-bounds characters in cookie names, paths and domains

## [3.7.0] - 2025-10-08

### Added
- `app.group(prefix, fn)` for grouping routes under a shared prefix
- Typed `ctx.params` for string-literal route paths, e.g. `"/users/:id"` gives `{ id: string }`

### Changed
- The logger middleware emits JSON by default when `NODE_ENV=production`

### Fixed
- `ctx.text()` responses were missing `charset=utf-8` in the `Content-Type` header

[4.2.0]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.1.1...v4.2.0
[4.1.1]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.1.0...v4.1.1
[4.1.0]: https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/compare/v4.0.0...v4.1.0

# Release Notes

Quarry follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) for its notebook format and plugin API; the user interface may change in any minor release. Notes for versions before 3.0 are archived on [the website](https://quarry.app/releases/archive).

## Quarry 3.4 — "Basalt" (November 3, 2026)

This release is mostly about speed. We rewrote the result grid from scratch on top of a virtualized canvas renderer, which means scrolling through a million-row result set now feels the same as scrolling through a hundred rows, and memory usage for large results dropped by roughly 70% in our benchmarks. If you've ever watched Quarry freeze for a few seconds after running `SELECT * FROM events` against a production replica (we have, many times), this one's for you.

The other big change is that notebooks can now have *parameters*. Declare a parameter in the notebook settings, reference it in any cell as `{{ start_date }}`, and Quarry renders a small form at the top of the notebook and re-runs dependent cells when a value changes. Parameters are always sent to the database as bind variables, never spliced into the SQL text, so there's no injection risk even when the value comes from a free-text field.

- New result grid with virtual scrolling, column pinning and per-column number formats
- Notebook parameters: text, number, date, date range, and "choice from query"
- `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E` exports the current result to CSV, Parquet or XLSX without opening a dialog
- ClickHouse driver now supports the native `JSON` column type
- **Breaking:** the `quarry.grid.maxRows` setting has been removed, since the new grid has no hard limit. If you relied on it as a safety net, use the per-connection *row limit* instead.
- Fixed: copying a cell that contains a newline produced invalid TSV on Windows

> **Heads up, plugin authors:** the `ResultView` extension point now receives an Apache Arrow `RecordBatch` instead of an array of row objects. A compatibility shim is in place for 3.4 and 3.5 and will be removed in 3.6.

## Quarry 3.3.2 (September 22, 2026)

A small bug-fix release. The most important fix is for a crash on startup on macOS when the login keychain was locked, which affected people who had "Store passwords in the system keychain" enabled and connected to their Mac over screen sharing. Thanks to everyone who sent crash reports, and especially to Hannes Kröger for bisecting it down to a single commit. 

* Fixed a crash on startup when the macOS keychain is locked
* Fixed autocomplete suggesting columns from the wrong schema when two schemas contain a table with the same name
* The Snowflake driver now honours `CLIENT_SESSION_KEEP_ALIVE`

## Quarry 3.3 (August 12, 2026)

Quarry 3.3 introduces __shared connections__ for teams. An admin defines a connection once — host, port, TLS settings, SSH tunnel, everything except the credentials — and publishes it to the workspace; teammates then add only their own username and password, or sign in with SSO. When the shared definition changes, everyone picks up the update the next time they connect. This has been the most requested feature on the forum two years running, and it turned out to be much harder to get right than we expected, mostly because of the many subtle ways an SSH tunnel configuration can differ between two machines.

We also shipped a long-overdue overhaul of query history. History is now searchable, can be filtered by connection and by outcome (succeeded, failed, cancelled), and records the execution time and row count of every query. It's stored locally and never leaves your machine unless you turn on sync.

- Shared connections (Team and Enterprise plans)
- Searchable, filterable query history
- New `EXPLAIN` visualizer for PostgreSQL and DuckDB, including per-node timings for `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
- **Breaking:** connection files (`.quarryconn`) saved by 3.3 can't be opened by 3.2 or earlier. The first time Quarry migrates a connection file, it keeps a backup of the original next to it.
- Dropped support for macOS 12 Monterey

> Note: this release bundles DuckDB 1.3. Database files created with older DuckDB versions are upgraded in place the first time you open them, so please back up any `.duckdb` files you care about before opening them in 3.3.

## Quarry 3.2.1 (June 30, 2026)

This release fixes a regression in 3.2 where the SQL formatter could move a trailing comment onto the following line, which in the worst case commented out part of a `WHERE` clause. **If you're on 3.2.0 and use "Format on run", please update right away.** We're sorry about this one. The formatter's test suite now includes several hundred real-world queries with comments in awkward places, and "Format on run" is now off by default for new installs, as it always should have been.

- Fixed the formatter moving trailing `--` comments onto the next line
- Fixed "Format on run" being enabled by default


## Quarry 3.2 (June 9, 2026)

The theme of 3.2 is _writing SQL faster_. Autocomplete now understands CTEs, subquery aliases and lateral joins, and ranks suggestions by how often you've used them on the current connection. There's a new built-in formatter (finally!) with a handful of options, and snippets can contain tab stops and placeholders using the same syntax as VS Code.

Under the hood, we moved the editor from CodeMirror 5 to CodeMirror 6. Most people won't notice anything except somewhat better performance on very long queries, but if you have customised keybindings, please double-check them: a few obscure Emacs-style bindings didn't survive the move.

* Context-aware autocomplete for CTEs, aliases and `LATERAL` joins
* Built-in SQL formatter (`Shift+Alt+F`)
* Snippets with tab stops and placeholders
* **Breaking:** custom keybindings that use CodeMirror 5 command names must be updated. Quarry shows a one-time notice listing any bindings it couldn't migrate automatically.
* Vim mode: `:s` substitutions now support the `g` and `c` flags

## Quarry 3.1 (April 2, 2026)

Quarry now runs natively on 64-bit ARM Linux, including the Raspberry Pi 5 and Asahi Linux on Apple Silicon Macs. We also added a portable Windows build that doesn't need administrator rights to install — something several people on locked-down corporate laptops had asked for.

- Linux ARM64 builds (`.deb`, `.rpm` and AppImage)
- Portable Windows build (`.zip`)
- BigQuery: authentication with workload identity federation

> If you installed the 3.1 beta from the AppImage, note that the stable release uses a different app ID.
> Your notebooks are safe, but you'll need to re-pin Quarry to your dock or taskbar.

## Quarry 3.0 (February 17, 2026)

Quarry 3.0 is the first release built on our new plugin architecture, and the first in which every database driver — including the built-in ones — is a plugin. That sounds like an internal detail, and mostly it is, but it means drivers can now be updated independently of the app, and third parties can publish drivers for databases we don't support ourselves. Within a week of the beta there were community drivers for CockroachDB, Trino and, somewhat to our surprise, Firebird.

The notebook format changed too. A 3.0 notebook is a plain Markdown file with fenced SQL code blocks and a small YAML header, so notebooks diff nicely in Git and render reasonably well on GitHub. Notebooks from Quarry 2.x (`.qnb`) are converted automatically when you open them; the original file is left untouched.

Finally, a word of thanks: 3.0 was in public beta for eleven weeks, and more than 1,400 of you sent feedback. A surprising number of the fixes in this release exist because someone took the time to write up exactly what they were doing when things went wrong. Thank you.

- **Breaking:** new notebook format (`.quarry.md`); 2.x notebooks are converted on open
- **Breaking:** the 2.x plugin API is not compatible with 3.0 — see the [migration guide](https://quarry.app/docs/plugins/migrating-to-3)
+ Driver marketplace with signed community drivers
+ Dark mode now follows the OS setting by default

# Contributing to Northwind UI

Thanks for taking the time to contribute! 🎉 This guide explains how to get the monorepo running locally, how we name branches and write commit messages, and what we look for in a pull request. If something here is unclear or out of date, please open an issue — or, even better, a PR that fixes it.

## Repository layout

```text
northwind-ui/
├── apps/
│   ├── docs/            # Docusaurus documentation site
│   └── playground/      # Vite sandbox for manual testing
├── packages/
│   ├── tokens/          # @northwind/tokens: design tokens (Style Dictionary)
│   ├── icons/           # @northwind/icons: SVG icon set + React components
│   ├── react/           # @northwind/react: the component library
│   └── eslint-config/   # @northwind/eslint-config (internal)
├── tooling/             # scripts, codemods, shared tsconfig
├── turbo.json
└── pnpm-workspace.yaml
```

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Version | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Node.js | 22.x (LTS) | `.nvmrc` is checked in; [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm) or [Volta](https://volta.sh) will pick it up automatically |
| pnpm | ≥ 9.12 | Enable it with `corepack enable`. Please **don't** install pnpm globally with npm, the versions drift |
| Git | ≥ 2.40 | |
| Playwright browsers | whatever `@playwright/test` pins | `pnpm test:e2e:install` |
| Docker | 24+ (optional) | Only needed to run the visual regression tests locally |

## Getting set up

1. Fork the repository and clone your fork:

   ```sh
   git clone git@github.com:<your-username>/northwind-ui.git
   cd northwind-ui
   ```

2. Install dependencies. This also installs the Git hooks via `lefthook`.

   ```sh
   corepack enable
   pnpm install
   ```

3. Build every package once so that cross-package imports resolve:
   ```sh
   pnpm build
   ```

4. Start the docs site and the playground in watch mode:

   ```sh
   pnpm dev --filter=docs --filter=playground
   ```

   The docs are served at http://localhost:3000 and the playground at http://localhost:5173.
5. Before pushing, run the same checks CI runs:

   ```sh
   pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test
   ```

> **Tip:** Turborepo caches task outputs, so a second `pnpm build` without changes should finish in a couple of seconds. If something looks stale, `pnpm clean` deletes every `dist/` folder and the local Turbo cache.

## Branch naming

Branch off `main` and use `<type>/<short-description>`, optionally including the issue number:

- `feat/combobox-async-options`
- `fix/1423-tooltip-flicker`
- `docs/theming-guide`
- `chore/bump-storybook-9`

The allowed types are the same as for commit messages (see below). Lowercase and hyphens only, and no more than one slash please — a couple of our CI scripts split on it.

## Commit messages

We use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). The scope is the package name without the `@northwind/` prefix (or `docs`, `playground`, `repo` for changes outside the packages). Messages are checked by `commitlint` in a Git hook and again in CI.

```text
feat(react): add `size` prop to <Avatar>

fix(tokens): correct contrast of color.text.subtle in dark theme

The previous value (#8b8f98 on #1b1d22) had a contrast ratio of 4.1:1,
which is below the WCAG AA threshold for body text.

Closes #1502

refactor(icons)!: rename IconClose to IconX

BREAKING CHANGE: IconClose has been removed. Run
`pnpm dlx @northwind/codemods icons-v3 src/` to update imports.
```

Allowed types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore` and `revert`.

## Pull request checklist

Before you request a review, please make sure that:

- [ ] the PR title follows the commit convention — we squash-merge, so the title becomes the commit message
- [ ] you've added a changeset (`pnpm changeset`) if the change affects a published package
- [ ] new components have stories in `*.stories.tsx` and pass the Storybook a11y checks
- [ ] tests cover the change (`pnpm test --filter=<package>`)
- [ ] public API changes are documented in `apps/docs`
- [ ] screenshots or a short screen recording are attached for visual changes
- [x] you've read this document 🙂

Small PRs get reviewed *much* faster than big ones. If your change touches more than one package, consider splitting it up.

## Style guide

### TypeScript

* Strict mode everywhere. Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` and narrow it.
* Export types with `export type { … }` so they're erased under `isolatedModules`.
* Named exports only. The single exception is Storybook story files, which need a default export.

### React components

- Function components only; forward refs with `React.forwardRef` and set a `displayName`.
- Props interfaces are called `<Component>Props` and are exported.
- Style with CSS Modules and tokens from `@northwind/tokens` — never hard-coded colors or spacing. Stylelint _will_ complain if you try `color: #333`.
- Every interactive component must be fully keyboard accessible and listed in the accessibility matrix in `apps/docs/docs/a11y.mdx`.

### CSS

Use logical properties (`margin-inline-start` rather than `margin-left`) so right-to-left layouts work out of the box. Class names in CSS Modules are `camelCase`.  

### Tests

Unit tests use Vitest and Testing Library. Query by role or label (`getByRole("button", { name: /save/i })`) rather than by test ID wherever possible — test IDs are a last resort, not a default.


## Release process

Maintainers cut releases from `main` using [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets).

1. Prepare
   1. Make sure `main` is green and every PR intended for the release has been merged.
   2. The changesets bot keeps a **Version Packages** PR open. Review the generated `CHANGELOG.md` entries and fix typos directly in that PR.
   3. For a major version, check that the migration guide in `apps/docs/docs/migrations/` is complete and linked from the changelog.
2. Publish
   1. Merge the Version Packages PR.
   2. The `release.yml` workflow builds every package, publishes to npm with provenance, and pushes tags such as `@northwind/react@3.2.0`.
   3. If publishing fails halfway through, __don't__ re-run the whole workflow. Run `pnpm release:resume` locally instead, with an npm token that has publish rights (ask in #northwind-maintainers).
3. Announce
   1. Post the release notes in #design-system and on the docs site's "What's new" page.
   2. Close the GitHub milestone and move anything left over to the next one.

Pre-releases on the `next` dist-tag follow the same steps on the `next` branch, after running `pnpm changeset pre enter next`.

## Questions?

Ask in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/northwind-ui/northwind-ui/discussions), or in `#northwind-ui` on Slack if you work here. We're happy to help!

> **Tip:** Turborepo caches task outputs, so a second `pnpm build` without changes should finish in a couple of seconds. If something looks stale, `pnpm clean` deletes every `dist/` folder and the local Turbo cache.

## Branch naming

Branch off `main` and use `<type>/<short-description>`, optionally including the issue number:

- `feat/combobox-async-options`
- `fix/1423-tooltip-flicker`
- `docs/theming-guide`
- `chore/bump-storybook-9`

The allowed types are the same as for commit messages (see below). Lowercase and hyphens only, and no more than one slash please — a couple of our CI scripts split on it.

## Commit messages

We use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). The scope is the package name without the `@northwind/` prefix (or `docs`, `playground`, `repo` for changes outside the packages). Messages are checked by `commitlint` in a Git hook and again in CI.

```text
feat(react): add `size` prop to <Avatar>

fix(tokens): correct contrast of color.text.subtle in dark theme

The previous value (#8b8f98 on #1b1d22) had a contrast ratio of 4.1:1,
which is below the WCAG AA threshold for body text.

Closes #1502

refactor(icons)!: rename IconClose to IconX

BREAKING CHANGE: IconClose has been removed. Run
`pnpm dlx @northwind/codemods icons-v3 src/` to update imports.
```

Allowed types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore` and `revert`.

## Pull request checklist

Before you request a review, please make sure that:

- [ ] the PR title follows the commit convention — we squash-merge, so the title becomes the commit message
- [ ] you've added a changeset (`pnpm changeset`) if the change affects a published package
- [ ] new components have stories in `*.stories.tsx` and pass the Storybook a11y checks
- [ ] tests cover the change (`pnpm test --filter=<package>`)
- [ ] public API changes are documented in `apps/docs`
- [ ] screenshots or a short screen recording are attached for visual changes
- [x] you've read this document 🙂

Small PRs get reviewed *much* faster than big ones. If your change touches more than one package, consider splitting it up.

## Style guide

### TypeScript

* Strict mode everywhere. Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` and narrow it.
* Export types with `export type { … }` so they're erased under `isolatedModules`.
* Named exports only. The single exception is Storybook story files, which need a default export.

### React components

- Function components only; forward refs with `React.forwardRef` and set a `displayName`.
- Props interfaces are called `<Component>Props` and are exported.
- Style with CSS Modules and tokens from `@northwind/tokens` — never hard-coded colors or spacing. Stylelint _will_ complain if you try `color: #333`.
- Every interactive component must be fully keyboard accessible and listed in the accessibility matrix in `apps/docs/docs/a11y.mdx`.

### CSS

Use logical properties (`margin-inline-start` rather than `margin-left`) so right-to-left layouts work out of the box. Class names in CSS Modules are `camelCase`.  

### Tests

Unit tests use Vitest and Testing Library. Query by role or label (`getByRole("button", { name: /save/i })`) rather than by test ID wherever possible — test IDs are a last resort, not a default.


## Release process

Maintainers cut releases from `main` using [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets).

1. Prepare
   1. Make sure `main` is green and every PR intended for the release has been merged.
   2. The changesets bot keeps a **Version Packages** PR open. Review the generated `CHANGELOG.md` entries and fix typos directly in that PR.
   3. For a major version, check that the migration guide in `apps/docs/docs/migrations/` is complete and linked from the changelog.
2. Publish
   1. Merge the Version Packages PR.
   2. The `release.yml` workflow builds every package, publishes to npm with provenance, and pushes tags such as `@northwind/react@3.2.0`.
   3. If publishing fails halfway through, __don't__ re-run the whole workflow. Run `pnpm release:resume` locally instead, with an npm token that has publish rights (ask in #northwind-maintainers).
3. Announce
   1. Post the release notes in #design-system and on the docs site's "What's new" page.
   2. Close the GitHub milestone and move anything left over to the next one.

Pre-releases on the `next` dist-tag follow the same steps on the `next` branch, after running `pnpm changeset pre enter next`.

## Questions?

Ask in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/northwind-ui/northwind-ui/discussions), or in `#northwind-ui` on Slack if you work here. We're happy to help!

# Contributing to OpenTrails

First of all: thank you. OpenTrails exists because thousands of hikers, mappers, park rangers and software developers decided that good trail information should be free for everyone, and every contribution, no matter how small, makes the map a little more accurate and a little more useful for the next person heading out the door with a backpack. Whether you walked a trail last weekend and noticed the bridge is out, or you're a seasoned Rust developer looking for an interesting routing problem, there's a place for you here.

This document is intentionally short. It covers the main ways to get involved and where to ask questions; the technical details (building the app, running the tile server, the data model) live in the [developer docs](https://docs.opentrails.org/dev/) so that they can be kept up to date in one place.

## Ways to contribute

You don't need to write code to make a big difference. Some of the most valuable contributions we get are:

* **Reporting trail conditions.** Closures, washed-out sections, new reroutes and seasonal restrictions change faster than any official source can keep up with. Use the "Report a condition" button in the app, or file an issue using the *Trail condition* template.
* **Improving the map data.** Our trail geometry comes from OpenStreetMap, so fixing a trail in OSM fixes it in OpenTrails within about a day. The [OSM hiking guide](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Hiking) is a great place to start.
* **Translating** the app and the website on [Weblate](https://hosted.weblate.org/projects/opentrails/). We currently ship in 27 languages, and about a dozen more are partially done.
* **Writing and editing documentation**, especially guides for first-time mappers.
* Triaging issues: reproducing bugs, adding missing details and labelling duplicates.
* **Code**, of course — the mobile apps (Kotlin and Swift), the routing engine (Rust), the web frontend (TypeScript and Svelte) and the data pipeline (Python).
- Spreading the word: giving talks, writing blog posts, or organising a mapping party in your area.

## Your first data fix in five minutes

If you've never edited OpenStreetMap before, here's the quickest way to fix a trail you know:

1. Find the trail on the OpenTrails web map and click **Edit on OSM** in the sidebar. This opens the iD editor centred on the right spot.
2. Log in, or create a free OSM account.
3. Select the trail and correct whatever is wrong: the name, the `sac_scale` difficulty, or the geometry itself.
4. Write a short changeset comment, such as "Fix trail name per signage at trailhead", and save.
5. That's it! Your change will show up in OpenTrails after the next nightly import.

Please only map what you've seen on the ground or can verify from a source with a compatible license. Copying from Google Maps, AllTrails or official park maps is _not_ allowed unless they explicitly permit it — we've had to revert whole regions because of this, which is heartbreaking for everyone involved. 

## Good first issues

If you'd like to contribute code but don't know where to start, look for issues labelled [`good first issue`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/good%20first%20issue). These are deliberately small, well-scoped tasks, typically a few hours of work for someone new to the codebase, and each one has a short description of where the relevant code lives and what a good solution might look like. A maintainer has committed to reviewing PRs for these issues within a few days, so you won't be left waiting.

Before starting, leave a comment on the issue saying you'd like to work on it, so that we can assign it to you and avoid two people doing the same thing. If you get stuck, that's completely normal: push what you have as a draft pull request and ask for help. We would much rather see an unfinished PR with a question than have you struggle silently for a week.

There's also a [`help wanted`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/help%20wanted) label for bigger tasks where we'd especially welcome outside help, and a [`local knowledge`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/local%20knowledge) label for issues that need someone who knows an area rather than someone who knows how to program.

## Making a pull request

Keep pull requests focused on one change, explain *why* in the description (the diff already shows *what*), and link the issue it addresses. Every PR is reviewed by at least one maintainer and needs passing CI before it's merged. We squash-merge, so don't worry about tidying up your commit history.


## Code of Conduct

Everyone participating in OpenTrails — on GitHub, in the forum, on Matrix, or at in-person events — is expected to follow our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), which is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1. In short: be kind, be patient with newcomers, assume good intent, and remember that most people here contribute in their spare time. Harassment of any kind is not tolerated.

If you experience or witness unacceptable behaviour, please report it to **conduct@opentrails.org**. Reports are handled confidentially by the community health team, which is separate from the core maintainers.

## Recognition

We use the [All Contributors](https://allcontributors.org) specification to recognise every kind of contribution, not just code. Once your first contribution has been merged, a maintainer will add you to the contributors list in the README; you can also ask the bot directly by commenting on any issue or pull request.

## Licensing

By contributing code, you agree that it will be licensed under the project's [AGPL-3.0](LICENSE) license. Documentation is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, and map data you add to OpenStreetMap is licensed under the ODbL by OSM itself.

## Getting in touch

- 💬 Chat: [#opentrails:matrix.org](https://matrix.to/#/#opentrails:matrix.org) (bridged to our Discord server)
- 🗣️ Forum: <https://community.opentrails.org>
- 🐘 Mastodon: [@opentrails@en.osm.town](https://en.osm.town/@opentrails)
- 📧 Email: hello@opentrails.org, for anything that doesn't fit elsewhere, including press and partnership enquiries
- 🔒 Security issues: please see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue

Maintainers are spread across time zones from Wellington to Vancouver, so please allow a day or two for a response.

Happy trails! 🥾

---
title: "Bike-Share Ridership Review: Q3 2026"
subtitle: "Weather, seasonality, and the first full quarter of the e-bike fleet"
author:
  - name: Priya Raman
    email: priya.raman@westbrook.gov
    affiliations: Mobility Analytics Unit, City of Westbrook
  - name: Tomás Ferreira
    affiliations: Mobility Analytics Unit, City of Westbrook
date: 2026-10-14
date-format: long
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    code-fold: true
    code-summary: "Show the code"
    theme: cosmo
    number-sections: true
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height: 4.5
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
jupyter: python3
bibliography: references.bib
---

## Summary

WestBike riders took **412,806 trips** between 1 July and 30 September 2026 — up 23.4% on Q3 2025 and the highest quarterly total since the system launched in 2019. About two thirds of that growth came from the 600 pedal-assist e-bikes added in June, which now account for 38% of trips despite making up only 22% of the fleet.[^fleet]

Key findings:

- Ridership remains strongly weather-dependent: a day with 5 mm of rain sees roughly a third fewer trips than a comparable dry day.
- E-bike trips are longer (median 14 min vs. 10 min) and more likely to start in the hillier eastern neighbourhoods.
* Casual riders made 21% of trips but generated 46% of fare revenue.
- The University and Riverside stations ran out of e-bikes before 08:15 on most weekday mornings.

[^fleet]: Fleet composition as of 30 September 2026: 2,140 classic bikes and 600 e-bikes. Bikes out of service for more than seven consecutive days are excluded from the denominator.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")

trips = pd.read_parquet("data/trips_2026q3.parquet")
weather = pd.read_csv("data/weather_daily_kwbk.csv", parse_dates=["date"])

daily = (
    trips.assign(date=trips["started_at"].dt.normalize())
    .groupby("date")
    .agg(trips=("trip_id", "size"), ebike_share=("is_ebike", "mean"))
    .reset_index()
    .merge(weather, on="date", how="left")
)
```

## Daily ridership

```{python}
#| label: fig-daily
#| fig-cap: "Daily trips, July–September 2026. The dashed line is the centred 7-day rolling mean; dark bars mark days with more than 5 mm of precipitation."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
wet = daily["precip_mm"] > 5
ax.bar(daily["date"], daily["trips"], color=np.where(wet, "#3182bd", "#9ecae1"), width=0.9)
ax.plot(daily["date"], daily["trips"].rolling(7, center=True).mean(), "k--", lw=1.5, label="7-day mean")
ax.set_ylabel("Trips per day")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

@fig-daily shows the usual summer plateau, a dip over the Fourth of July weekend, and a sharp drop on 11–12 September, when the remnants of Tropical Storm Fiona closed the system for 31 hours.


::: {.callout-tip}
## Reproducing this report

All inputs live in the `mobility-data` bucket under `bikeshare/2026q3/`. Run `quarto render ridership_q3.qmd` from the repository root after `uv sync`. Rendering takes about two minutes, most of it spent fitting the model in @sec-model; set `QUARTO_PYTHON` if you have more than one Python installation.
:::

## Patterns of use

::: {.panel-tabset}

### By hour

```{python}
#| label: fig-hourly
#| fig-cap: "Share of trips by hour of day, weekdays vs. weekends."
hourly = (
    trips.assign(hour=trips["started_at"].dt.hour,
                 weekend=trips["started_at"].dt.dayofweek >= 5)
    .groupby(["weekend", "hour"]).size().unstack(0)
)
hourly.columns = ["Weekday", "Weekend"]
(hourly / hourly.sum()).plot(xlabel="Hour of day", ylabel="Share of trips")
plt.show()
```

Weekday use is sharply bimodal, peaking at 08:00 and 17:00. On weekends, use climbs gradually to a broad peak in the early afternoon.

### By weekday

```{python}
#| label: fig-weekday
#| fig-cap: "Mean trips per day of the week."
order = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
daily.groupby(daily["date"].dt.day_name())["trips"].mean().reindex(order).plot(kind="bar", xlabel="", ylabel="Mean trips per day")
plt.show()
```

### By membership

| Rider type | Trips | Share | Median duration |
|:-----------|------:|------:|----------------:|
| Annual member | 268,324 | 65.0% | 11 min |
| Monthly pass | 57,793 | 14.0% | 13 min |
| Day pass / single ride | 86,689 | 21.0% | 24 min|

Casual riders take fewer but longer trips, and are _far_ more likely to start and end at the same station.

:::

## Weather model {#sec-model}

To separate the effect of weather from the seasonal trend, we fit a Poisson regression with a log link to the daily trip counts $Y_t$:

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_t + \beta_2 T_t^2 + \beta_3 \log(1 + P_t) + \sum_{d=1}^{6} \gamma_d \, \mathbb{1}[\mathrm{dow}_t = d] + \delta H_t
$$ {#eq-poisson}

where $T_t$ is the daily maximum temperature in °C, $P_t$ the precipitation in mm, and $H_t$ a public-holiday indicator. Overdispersion was modest (Pearson $\chi^2/\text{df} = 1.8$), so the standard errors in @tbl-coefs come from a quasi-Poisson fit.

```{python}
#| label: model
model = smf.glm(
    "trips ~ tmax + I(tmax**2) + np.log1p(precip_mm) + C(dow) + holiday",
    data=daily.assign(dow=daily["date"].dt.dayofweek),
    family=sm.families.Poisson(),
).fit(scale="X2")
```

| Term | Estimate | Std. error | Rate ratio |
|------|---------:|-----------:|-----------:|
| $T_t$ (°C) | 0.061 | 0.011 | 1.063 |
| $T_t^2$ | −0.0012 | 0.0003 | 0.999 |
| $\log(1 + P_t)$ | −0.214 | 0.019 | 0.807 |
| Holiday | −0.152 | 0.047 | 0.859 |

: Selected coefficients from @eq-poisson; day-of-week effects omitted for brevity. {#tbl-coefs}

The temperature effect is concave, with expected ridership peaking at around 25 °C, consistent with earlier studies of North American systems [@gebhart2014impact; @noland2016bikeshare]. Holding everything else fixed, a day with 10 mm of rain has an expected count about $1 - 0.807^{\ln 11} \approx 40\%$ lower than a dry day.[^rain]

[^rain]: Because precipitation enters the model as $\log(1 + P_t)$, each additional millimetre matters less than the one before. Riders who are already out in 10 mm of rain, apparently, don't much mind 15.

## Recommendations

1. Rebalance e-bikes toward the University and Riverside stations before 07:30 on weekdays; both run empty by 08:15 on 71% of weekdays.
2. Pilot weather-responsive pricing for casual riders, which @noland2016bikeshare suggest can smooth demand without reducing total trips.
3. Expand the e-bike fleet only *after* charging capacity at the Harbour Street depot is upgraded (see the separate capital plan, item CP-27-114).

## References

::: {#refs}
:::

    .groupby(["weekend", "hour"]).size().unstack(0)
)
hourly.columns = ["Weekday", "Weekend"]
(hourly / hourly.sum()).plot(xlabel="Hour of day", ylabel="Share of trips")
plt.show()
```

Weekday use is sharply bimodal, peaking at 08:00 and 17:00. On weekends, use climbs gradually to a broad peak in the early afternoon.

### By weekday

```{python}
#| label: fig-weekday
#| fig-cap: "Mean trips per day of the week."
order = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
daily.groupby(daily["date"].dt.day_name())["trips"].mean().reindex(order).plot(kind="bar", xlabel="", ylabel="Mean trips per day")
plt.show()
```

### By membership

| Rider type | Trips | Share | Median duration |
|:-----------|------:|------:|----------------:|
| Annual member | 268,324 | 65.0% | 11 min |
| Monthly pass | 57,793 | 14.0% | 13 min |
| Day pass / single ride | 86,689 | 21.0% | 24 min|

Casual riders take fewer but longer trips, and are _far_ more likely to start and end at the same station.

:::

## Weather model {#sec-model}

To separate the effect of weather from the seasonal trend, we fit a Poisson regression with a log link to the daily trip counts $Y_t$:

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_t + \beta_2 T_t^2 + \beta_3 \log(1 + P_t) + \sum_{d=1}^{6} \gamma_d \, \mathbb{1}[\mathrm{dow}_t = d] + \delta H_t
$$ {#eq-poisson}

where $T_t$ is the daily maximum temperature in °C, $P_t$ the precipitation in mm, and $H_t$ a public-holiday indicator. Overdispersion was modest (Pearson $\chi^2/\text{df} = 1.8$), so the standard errors in @tbl-coefs come from a quasi-Poisson fit.

```{python}
#| label: model
model = smf.glm(
    "trips ~ tmax + I(tmax**2) + np.log1p(precip_mm) + C(dow) + holiday",
    data=daily.assign(dow=daily["date"].dt.dayofweek),
    family=sm.families.Poisson(),
).fit(scale="X2")
```

| Term | Estimate | Std. error | Rate ratio |
|------|---------:|-----------:|-----------:|
| $T_t$ (°C) | 0.061 | 0.011 | 1.063 |
| $T_t^2$ | −0.0012 | 0.0003 | 0.999 |
| $\log(1 + P_t)$ | −0.214 | 0.019 | 0.807 |
| Holiday | −0.152 | 0.047 | 0.859 |

: Selected coefficients from @eq-poisson; day-of-week effects omitted for brevity. {#tbl-coefs}

The temperature effect is concave, with expected ridership peaking at around 25 °C, consistent with earlier studies of North American systems [@gebhart2014impact; @noland2016bikeshare]. Holding everything else fixed, a day with 10 mm of rain has an expected count about $1 - 0.807^{\ln 11} \approx 40\%$ lower than a dry day.[^rain]

[^rain]: Because precipitation enters the model as $\log(1 + P_t)$, each additional millimetre matters less than the one before. Riders who are already out in 10 mm of rain, apparently, don't much mind 15.

## Recommendations

1. Rebalance e-bikes toward the University and Riverside stations before 07:30 on weekdays; both run empty by 08:15 on 71% of weekdays.
2. Pilot weather-responsive pricing for casual riders, which @noland2016bikeshare suggest can smooth demand without reducing total trips.
3. Expand the e-bike fleet only *after* charging capacity at the Harbour Street depot is upgraded (see the separate capital plan, item CP-27-114).

## References

::: {#refs}
:::

---
title: "From Makefiles to `{targets}`"
subtitle: "How we made the weekly forecast pipeline reproducible (and a lot faster)"
author: "Lena Hoffmann"
institute: "Data Science Guild"
date: 2026-11-05
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: [default, custom.scss]
    slide-number: c/t
    logo: images/guild-logo.png
    footer: "Data Science Guild · November 2026"
    code-overflow: wrap
    transition: fade
    chalkboard: true
    preview-links: auto
execute:
  echo: true
  eval: false
---

## Where we started

![](images/pipeline-before.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" fig-alt="A tangle of fourteen R scripts connected by arrows, several of them labelled 'run manually'"}

::: {.notes}
Open with the diagram and ask: who has a folder called `final_v2_REAL`? Pause for laughs.

The point is: 14 scripts, run in an order only Marco knew, and Marco is on parental leave until March.
:::

## What hurt

::: {.incremental}
- Re-running *everything* after a one-line change (~3 hours)
- "Works on my machine" — different package versions on every laptop
- No way to tell which outputs were stale
- The Monday report silently used **last week's** data. Twice.
:::

::: {.notes}
The stale-data incident is what got us the budget for this. Don't dwell on it — the people involved are in the room.
:::

## What `{targets}` gives you

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A declarative pipeline**

- each step is a *target*: a name plus a command
- dependencies are found by static code analysis
- only outdated targets re-run
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
__More or less for free__

* parallel workers via `{crew}`
* targets stored in the cloud (S3, GCS)
* a dependency graph: `tar_visnetwork()`
:::

::::

## A minimal `_targets.R`

```{.r code-line-numbers="2-3"}
library(targets)
tar_option_set(packages = c("dplyr", "readr", "fable"))
tar_source("R/")

list(
  tar_target(raw_file, "data/sales.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(sales, read_sales(raw_file)),
  tar_target(model, fit_models(sales)),
  tar_target(forecast, make_forecast(model, h = "8 weeks"))
)
```

::: {.notes}
Lines 2–3 first: packages, and sourcing our own functions from `R/`.
Then the pipeline itself is just a list. Emphasise `format = "file"` — that's what makes the CSV a tracked dependency, so editing the file triggers a rebuild of everything downstream.
:::

## Running it

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3"}
tar_make()
#> ▶ dispatched target sales
tar_visnetwork(targets_only = TRUE)
```

![](images/visnetwork.png){.r-stretch fig-alt="Dependency graph rendered by tar_visnetwork, with outdated targets highlighted in blue"}

## Making it fast

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.incremental}
- branch over stores with `pattern = map()`
- 8 local workers with `{crew}`
- cache on a shared S3 bucket
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{.r code-line-numbers="2|5-6"}
tar_option_set(
  controller = crew::crew_controller_local(workers = 8)
)
tar_target(
  model, fit_models(sales_by_store),
  pattern = map(sales_by_store)
)
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Dynamic branching: one model per store, 212 stores. With 8 workers the model step goes from ~2 h to ~20 min.
:::

## Results

| | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Full run | 3 h 10 min | 46 min |
| Typical Monday run | 3 h 10 min | **4 min** |
| Stale outputs in report | ¯\\\_(ツ)\_/¯ | 0 |

::: {.notes}
"Typical Monday run" = only the newest week of data changes, so most targets are skipped.
The shrug is deliberate. Wait for the laugh.
:::


## Lessons learned {.smaller}

1. Write *functions* first. The pipeline is just glue.
2. Keep targets small enough to be cheap to rebuild, but big enough to mean something
3. Use `format = "file"` for anything read from disk
4. Don't put secrets in `_targets.R` — use `.Renviron`
5. `tar_meta()` is your friend when debugging "why did this re-run?"

## Questions? {background-color="#1d3557"}

![](images/qr-repo.png){width="220" fig-align="right" fig-alt="QR code linking to the talk repository"}

Slides and code: <https://github.com/ds-guild/targets-talk>
Slack: `#guild-reproducibility`

::: {.notes}
If there are no questions, jump to the appendix slide on S3 costs.
:::

## Appendix: S3 costs {visibility="uncounted"}

About **$4.20 per month** for ~38 GB of stored targets, almost all of it forecast objects.

---
title: "Urban heat and pollinator visitation in community gardens"
author:
  - Amara Nwosu
  - Felix Bergström
  - Rosa I. Delgado
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    number_sections: true
    df_print: kable
bibliography: references.bib
csl: ecology.csl
link-citations: true
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
  chunk_output_type: console
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(broom.mixed)

visits  <- read_csv("data/visits_2025.csv")
gardens <- read_csv("data/gardens.csv")

n_gardens <- n_distinct(visits$garden_id)
n_obs     <- nrow(visits)
mean_uhi  <- mean(gardens$uhi_intensity, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Introduction

Cities are warmer than the landscapes around them.
This urban heat island (UHI) effect is typically 1--3 °C on average, but can exceed 7 °C on calm, clear summer nights [@oke1982energetic; @zhao2014strong, p. 217].
Insect pollinators are ectotherms, i.e. their activity depends directly on ambient temperature, so the UHI may change when and how often they visit flowers.

Earlier studies have produced mixed results. Hamblin et al. [-@hamblin2018physiological] found that large-bodied bees declined in abundance along an urban warming gradient in Raleigh, NC, whereas small-bodied taxa were largely unaffected; by contrast, a survey of 12 gardens in Berlin found no detectable effect of local temperature on visitation once floral abundance was accounted for [@vonkonigslow2022; but see @theodorou2020urban]. Most of this work has relied on temperature data from airport weather stations approx. 10--20 km from the study sites, which cannot capture the fine-scale variation that matters to a foraging bee [@hamblin2018physiological; @burdine2019, p. 4].

Here we ask three questions:

* Does garden-level UHI intensity predict pollinator visitation rates?
* Is the relationship different for bees vs. hoverflies?
* Does the effect depend on the time of day, e.g. is it stronger during the afternoon heat?

# Methods

## Study sites

We surveyed `r n_gardens` community gardens across Greater Manchester, UK, between 1 June and 31 August 2025.
Gardens were chosen to span a gradient of impervious surface cover (12.5--81.0 % within a 500 m buffer) while keeping garden size roughly constant (median 0.21 ha, range 0.08--0.46 ha).
Mean UHI intensity across gardens was `r round(mean_uhi, 2)` °C; see Fig. 1 for the full distribution.

## Temperature measurements

Each garden was fitted with two iButton DS1923 loggers in radiation shields at 1.5 m height, recording every 30 min. Loggers were calibrated against a reference thermometer before and after the field season, and drift was < 0.2 °C in all cases. UHI intensity was defined as the mean difference between garden temperature and a rural reference site at Abbots Moss^[Open heathland approx. 40 km SW of Manchester city centre, at a similar elevation to the study gardens.] between 10:00 and 16:00, i.e. the hours during which surveys took place.

## Pollinator surveys

Visitation was recorded in 10-min timed observations of a standardised 1 m² patch of *Borago officinalis* planted in each garden in April.
Observers recorded every insect that contacted the anthers or stigma and identified it to the lowest practical taxonomic level (usually genus for bees, family for flies).
Each garden was surveyed on 9 dates, three times per date (morning, midday, afternoon), giving `r n_obs` observation periods in total.

## Statistical analysis

We modelled visit counts with a Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a log link [@bates2015lme4]. In brief:

- response: number of visits per 10-min observation
- fixed effects: UHI intensity (°C), pollinator group, survey period, and the group × UHI and period × UHI interactions
+ offset: log number of open flowers in the patch
- random intercepts: garden and survey date

All analyses were done in R version `r getRversion()` [@rcore2025].

```{r model, echo=TRUE}
m1 <- glmer(
  visits ~ uhi_intensity * group + uhi_intensity * period + offset(log(n_flowers)) +
    (1 | garden_id) + (1 | survey_date),
  data = visits, family = poisson,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)
coefs <- tidy(m1, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE)
b_uhi <- coefs |> filter(term == "uhi_intensity") |> pull(estimate)
```

# Results

We recorded 4,318 flower visits, of which 61.4 % were by bees (mainly *Bombus* spp. and *Apis mellifera*) and 29.8 % by hoverflies (Syrphidae).
The remaining 8.8 % were by other flies, butterflies and the occasional wasp.

Visitation increased with UHI intensity overall (β = `r round(b_uhi, 2)` per °C), but the effect differed strongly between groups (Fig. 2). For bees, each additional degree of UHI intensity was associated with approx. 14 % more visits per flower (rate ratio 1.14, 95 % CI 1.05--1.24), whereas for hoverflies the estimate was close to zero and slightly negative (RR 0.97, 95 % CI 0.86--1.09). The interaction with survey period was weak. If anything, the positive effect for bees was _smaller_ in the afternoon than in the morning, contrary to our expectation!

```{r fig-visits, fig.cap="Fig. 2: Predicted visits per 100 flowers per 10 min vs. UHI intensity, by pollinator group (midday surveys). Ribbons show 95 % confidence intervals."}
newdat <- expand_grid(
  uhi_intensity = seq(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), max(gardens$uhi_intensity), length.out = 50),
  group = c("bee", "hoverfly"), period = "midday", n_flowers = 100
)
newdat$pred <- predict(m1, newdata = newdat, re.form = NA, type = "response")
ggplot(newdat, aes(uhi_intensity, pred, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "UHI intensity (°C)", y = "Visits per 100 flowers per 10 min", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Discussion

Our results suggest that moderate urban warming may benefit bees in a temperate maritime climate, where cool and cloudy days frequently limit foraging.
This is consistent with the thermal-limitation hypothesis [@kuhsel2015high] and with observations of earlier activity onset in warmer microsites [@fisogni2020; @kammerer2021, pp. 3--5].
Hoverflies, in contrast, did not respond to warming, possibly because many syrphids tolerate low temperatures better than bees do.[^1]

There are several caveats. First, our temperature gradient (`r round(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)`--`r round(max(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)` °C) is modest compared with cities in continental or Mediterranean climates, and the relationship may well reverse above some threshold, e.g. once afternoon temperatures regularly exceed 30 °C. Second, we measured visitation, not pollination effectiveness or bee fitness. Third, 2025 was an unusually warm summer in the UK, which may have compressed the range of conditions we sampled.

Future work should combine fine-scale temperature monitoring with measurements of pollen deposition and pollinator body condition, ideally across several years and cities.


[^1]: Several common UK hoverflies, e.g. *Episyrphus balteatus*, are active at air temperatures as low as 10 °C, whereas most bumblebees must warm their flight muscles to approx. 30 °C before take-off.

# Acknowledgements {.unnumbered}

We thank the 23 garden groups who hosted loggers and borage patches, and the volunteers who spent approx. 300 hours watching flowers.
Funded by NERC grant NE/X012345/1.

# References {.unnumbered}

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "UHI intensity (°C)", y = "Visits per 100 flowers per 10 min", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Discussion

Our results suggest that moderate urban warming may benefit bees in a temperate maritime climate, where cool and cloudy days frequently limit foraging.
This is consistent with the thermal-limitation hypothesis [@kuhsel2015high] and with observations of earlier activity onset in warmer microsites [@fisogni2020; @kammerer2021, pp. 3--5].
Hoverflies, in contrast, did not respond to warming, possibly because many syrphids tolerate low temperatures better than bees do.[^1]

There are several caveats. First, our temperature gradient (`r round(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)`--`r round(max(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)` °C) is modest compared with cities in continental or Mediterranean climates, and the relationship may well reverse above some threshold, e.g. once afternoon temperatures regularly exceed 30 °C. Second, we measured visitation, not pollination effectiveness or bee fitness. Third, 2025 was an unusually warm summer in the UK, which may have compressed the range of conditions we sampled.

Future work should combine fine-scale temperature monitoring with measurements of pollen deposition and pollinator body condition, ideally across several years and cities.

output:
